#5283. LINK, AAVE and UNI Now Supported by Fidelity

Fidelity Investments now supports three new cryptocurrencies on its retail crypto trading platform: Chainlink (LINK), Aave (AAVE) and Uniswap (UNI).

The firm expanded from five available cryptocurrencies to eight on Nov. 24. In just one day, Fidelity added the same number of digital assets that it had added in the four years since it first made Bitcoin and Ether available for customer trading.

Eligible U.S. customers can trade these three tokens on the Fidelity website and app. Some states may have limited access to Fidelity's services.

Fidelity's three new listings include tokens that represent different areas of decentralized finance. Aave is a lending protocol where users can deposit crypto assets to earn interest or use them as collateral for loans. AAVE token holders can vote on changes to the protocol's lending markets and other aspects of its operation.

Uniswap is a decentralized trading platform where users can trade different tokens using shared pools of assets provided by other users. UNI is the Uniswap governance token.

Chainlink provides the data that blockchain apps need to operate. For example, a lending protocol might use a Chainlink price feed to assess the value of collateral for a borrower's loan. Chainlink (LINK) tokens are used to pay for services provided on its network.

Fidelity Crypto started accepting customers from its waitlist in November 2022. At the time, the only two cryptocurrencies it offered were Bitcoin (BTC) and Ether (ETH). By March 2023, Fidelity was offering its service to more eligible U.S. investors, but these were still the only cryptocurrencies it allowed customers to trade.

On July 17, 2024, Fidelity added Litecoin (LTC) to its list of cryptocurrencies, bringing the total to three. Over a year later, on Oct. 23, 2025, the company introduced Solana (SOL). In addition to individual retail accounts, Solana became available for crypto IRAs, wealth managers and institutional clients.

Fidelity added its fifth cryptocurrency on Feb. 4, 2026, when it launched Fidelity Digital Dollar (FIDD) as its first stablecoin available to retail and institutional investors. Eligible users can exchange or redeem each FIDD token for $1. Fidelity waives its usual crypto trading fee when users exchange FIDD for dollars.

#5282. Your AI Startup’s Exit Is Being Shaped By The Deals You Sign Today

Valuations for AI companies have soared, and the companies are moving faster than ever. In the financings our firm has worked on so far in 2026, AI companies raised at median pre-money valuations up to 2.5 times those of non-AI companies from seed through Series C.

Across the broader private market, Crunchbase’s Current Valuation Model estimates that the more than 1,900 startups on its Unicorn Board are worth about $2 trillion more collectively than their last reported funding-round valuations.

When everything moves that fast, the terms of your financings and of your contracts for compute, data and distribution get set early and in a hurry. Some of those terms will later slow a sale, add cost and erode value. The key is making sure you take long enough to consider what a deal does to your exit before you sign.

Take license-and-hire deals, where a buyer licenses your technology and hires your team instead of acquiring the company. They’ve become more common in AI, and the National Venture Capital Association has responded by updating its model charter. In 2025, it added an optional investor approval right over these deals, and sign-off by the board, including the investors’ directors, was enough to satisfy it.

The November 2026 update requires a vote of the preferred stockholders instead. Investors are often reluctant to use an approval right to block a deal. But it puts them at the negotiating table when an offer arrives, with a voice in how the proceeds are split between retention packages for the team and the cap table.

The stakes are higher when an investor is also a strategic partner. Nvidia and its NVentures investment arm alone have invested in more than 260 startups since the beginning of 2024, including 121 this year alone, Crunchbase data shows.

Strategic capital often comes tied to compute, cloud or distribution agreements. Those agreements can carry exclusivity, change-of-control and right-of-first-negotiation terms, and a right of first negotiation can force you to put a competing bidder on ice while you talk to your strategic investor first.

Be realistic about your leverage. Terms from the hottest AI rounds get cited as “market,” but what you can get depends on how much investors want your deal. Spend your negotiating capital on the few provisions that will matter most in a sale instead of trying to optimize on marginal topics.

An AI company’s most valuable assets are often the hardest to diligence.

Start with data. A buyer will want to know where your training data came from and whether your contractual rights cover how you use it and how the buyer plans to use it. Publicly available data isn’t necessarily licensed data. And permission to use a customer’s data to serve that customer doesn’t always cover training models for everyone else. If you fine-tuned on customer data under contracts that limit its use to serving those customers, a buyer may not be able to fold your models into its own products. The buyer may ask for a special indemnity, a larger escrow or a lower purchase price.

Your code gets similar scrutiny. In our deals, investors, and especially acquirers, now ask how much of the codebase was written with AI tools and whether those tools pulled in copyleft or commercially licensed code. We tell clients to audit their code regularly and fix issues as they surface. It makes that diligence conversation far easier.

Compute and model-provider contracts raise a different problem: a buyer may inherit a commitment it doesn’t want. Minimum-spend commitments, reserved capacity and exclusivity terms generally stay with the company in a sale. A buyer with its own GPUs may have no use for three more years of your reserved capacity, and it will factor the remaining payments into its offer.

All of this is easier to fix at the negotiating table than in the middle of a buyer’s diligence.

• Map who decides on a sale. Know which board and investor approvals it would trigger, including any approval right over a license-and-hire deal.

• Track your data and code rights. Record data sources and use restrictions and audit AI-generated code periodically.

• Stress-test your infrastructure commitments. Run cloud, GPU and model-provider obligations against slower growth and a sale.

• Keep strategic rights narrow. Limit the scope, duration and triggers of any right of first offer or negotiation you give a strategic investor.

• Read commercial contracts with an exit in mind. Check the change-of-control and termination rights before you sign.

Few founders are thinking about a sale when they close a seed round or sign their first GPU contract. You don’t have to predict the exit. You do have to know what you’re giving up each time you sign, so the speed that got you funded doesn’t cost you flexibility when the right acquisition offer arrives.

Aaron Rubin is a partner in Gunderson Dettmer’s Strategic Transactions & Licensing group and a leader of the firm’s artificial intelligence practice. He advises AI companies on strategic partnerships, technology and data licensing, and the development, commercialization, and deployment of AI products and services. His practice spans complex commercial transactions, intellectual property and data rights, and the evolving legal and regulatory issues shaping the AI industry. He also advises leading investors in industry-defining AI financings, including investments in Anthropic, OpenAI, and Databricks.

Greg Volkmar is head of Gunderson Dettmer’s New York corporate group and co-chairs the firm’s growth equity practice. For more than 20 years, Volkmar has focused on advising early- and late-stage technology and life science companies through financings, corporate governance, and securities law matters. He is also a trusted advisor to leading venture capital, private equity and crossover funds on their US and global investment activities, such as equity and debt financings, mergers and acquisitions, and secondary liquidity transactions, as well as fund formation needs.

#5281. XRP News: Thanksgiving Rally or December 1 Supply Shock?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

XRP has a history of making Thanksgiving interesting, old news for some. In 2024, Ripple surged nearly 49% in the three days following the holiday. Last year, it went nowhere. Now, XRP is heading into another Thanksgiving with $1 in sight and Ripple’s 1 billion-token escrow unlock looming on December 1.

The timing puts bulls in a tight spot. XRP is recovering from a November sell-off, but the rebound has yet to clear major resistance. A holiday rally could give buyers some breathing room before next week’s token release puts supply back in the spotlight.

The 2024 Thanksgiving weekend was anything but quiet for XRP. The token closed November 28 at $1.54, climbed to $1.80 the following day, and reached $2.29 by December 1. That was a gain of nearly 49% from Thanksgiving’s close.

The rally had fuel beyond holiday trading as Donald Trump’s election victory revived hopes for a friendlier crypto regulatory environment, while XRP was breaking out after years of being held back by its SEC lawsuit. Buyers were chasing momentum, and the long weekend did little to slow them down.

Last year’s price action was considerably less exciting. XRP closed Thanksgiving on November 27, 2025, near $2.20, then drifted around $2.16 over the following days. The market offered no repeat of the explosive move seen a year earlier.

That history makes this year’s comparison interesting, but the conditions are different. XRP is entering Thanksgiving after a painful November decline.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

XRP’s recovery toward $0.95 has brought the psychological $1 level back into play. Buyers have been defending the area below $0.90, preventing another immediate breakdown and giving the short-term chart some breathing room.

But the problem is overhead resistance, as XRP must first push through $0.96–$0.98 before $1 becomes a realistic breakout target. That zone has become the immediate test for buyers. A clean move through it could attract momentum traders and open the path toward $1.02 and $1.08.

The $1 mark matters because XRP has spent November losing ground. Reclaiming it would put the token back above an important psychological threshold and give bulls something concrete to work with.

Failure to break resistance could leave the rebound looking like another dead-cat bounce. XRP’s recent low around $0.89 remains the level to watch. Losing it would put $0.86 back on the radar and risk undoing the recovery.

For now, the chart is caught between an improving short-term bounce and a damaged larger trend. Bulls have a chance, but they need to turn that chance into a breakout.

The next complication arrives Monday, with Ripple’s scheduled escrow contracts. It will release 1 billion XRP, renewing concerns about supply just as the token tries to recover from bad geopolitical news.

The billion-token headline sounds worse than Ripple’s typical net release. Over the past year, the company has re-escrowed around 70% of monthly unlocks, leaving around 300 million XRP outside escrow on average. The market will be watching whether December follows the same pattern.

The full 1 billion XRP unlock is not equivalent to 1 billion tokens hitting exchanges for sale. What Ripple re-locks, retains, or moves afterward will determine how much circulating supply actually changes.

What does it need? XRP cannot afford to enter Monday with a failed breakout and weakening support. If buyers reclaim $1 before the unlock, sentiment could shift in their favor. If XRP remains pinned below resistance, the escrow event gives nervous traders another reason to stay cautious.

Thanksgiving delivered XRP a spectacular rally in 2024. This year, bulls need more than a holiday repeat; they need the $1 back.

#5278. End of Crypto Trading? How AI Replaces Ones Who Pumped Bitcoin (BTC)

The “pump” trade could be taken to new extremes. While some may still be able to use their influence to promote a token, causing others to pile in, it could now be left up to AI to scour socials/wallet activity for abnormal trading volume, assess momentum rankings, etc. and execute on these opportunities faster than those that may be slower to react.

All things considered, agents may exacerbate many of the existing issues with crypto, from short lived moves/reversals, to dangerous herding and even more pronounced drawdowns.

Automation is not necessarily a new occurrence in the space, from simple rule-based trading (implement a certain set of rules when X occurs) to algo trading (use algos to spread out trading activity to avoid market impact), but it appears to be shifting from humans implementing strategies to letting AI make decisions and execute.

A February 2026 study from the Journal of Futures Markets found sub-second trading patterns in BTC/ETH perpetual/spot markets exhibiting behavior consistent with algo trading for liquidity, increasing volatility and trading costs with no significant impact on prices.

In August 2026, Binance rolled out Agent OS allowing builders to access exchange trading functionality and data via AI agents.

Coinbase Ventures released a comprehensive breakdown of the crypto agentic stack from data, to agent building tools, to execution/compliance in November. Instead of dictating each trade, users may be able to assign high-level goals (i.e. follow momentum, hedge position, etc.) for agents to implement 24/7.

Automation will likely accelerate across the crypto space. While macro events, ETF inflows/outflows, large holders, etc. will still have an impact on Bitcoin, it’s likely that many more aspects/trades will become automated.

Time will tell how pervasive agentic trading will become, but the era of a small group of traders/influencers/chat rooms able to move the needle via FOMO/hype seems poised to face stiff competition from AI that never sleeps.

AI is not necessarily intelligent. A 2026 study published in the journal Frontiers in Blockchain studied machine-learning strategies using crypto market data and found that many strategies became highly overfit and offered no viable edge for retail traders once realistic trading fees were taken into account.

Also, strategies that performed well on one cryptocurrency did not necessarily perform well on others. Faster processing speeds can’t make bad data good, can’t identify all false narratives and can’t insulate a strategy from sudden shifts in market regimes.

Are institutional investors still relevant? Can they protect themselves? Absolutely.

Institutions are (and will continue to be) an important source of capital, liquidity and price discovery (particularly for Bitcoin). A 2026 study using BTC data from 2012–2025 found that as the market has matured, Bitcoin has seen increased trading volume, decreasing transaction costs and increasing market efficiency.

Wintermute reported that in the first half of 2026 institutional clients accounted for 72% of total spot trading volume on its OTC desk (note: this is Wintermute’s OTC desk and is not representative of the entire market). It’s also worth noting that many institutional investors do employ quantitative strategies and state-of-the-art execution technologies.

While larger investors may have access to better data, faster infrastructure, cross-venue surveillance capabilities and stricter risk management protocols (and can limit their exposure and monitor abnormal order flow), there’s only so much that institutional investors can do to protect themselves.

Institutional investors can’t control a 24/7 global market with liquidity spread across multiple venues and derivatives markets. They also can’t assume that all AIs are created equal/safe (as Binance’s launch of its own AI demonstrated prompt injection risks and limited visibility into external AIs’ trading logic/reasons for trading).

Finally, during times of stress, risk management/contingency protocols (used by many investors) could be a crowded exit for funds that employ similar strategies.

The future is not “AI replaces every trader.” It will likely see continued automation of certain aspects of trading (i.e. execution, short-term alpha hunting, etc.) and a continued shift in the value-add that humans bring to the table (i.e. capital allocation, risk management, original research, granting/trading bots permission to trade, etc.).

While AI/bots may continue to squeeze spreads in normal market conditions, they may exacerbate drawdowns/cascades during times of market stress as strategies compete with one another.

At the end of the day, Bitcoin will still be bought/sold, it’s just a question of who gets to make those decisions.

#5277. Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game

A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

“So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

“A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.

What’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping users meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team says that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

Island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

The idea to encourage users to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

Similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup says Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active users-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

The app is currently free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

#5276. The Art of The Terrible Startup Name

When thinking of startup names, the usual question is how one identifies a great one.

But perhaps equally crucial is the reverse consideration: What makes for a truly awful startup name?

It’s a somewhat subjective exercise. Nonetheless, branding experts and occasional writers on the subject can agree on a few basic parameters. These include hard-sounding names, brands with negative connotations, and a certain ubiquitous suffix that could soon sound irrelevant.

Below, we look at each of these categories in more detail

One branding principle is that startups should avoid names that are unpleasant to pronounce. This includes words that sound too harsh or guttural, or are awkward in the native languages of potential users.

Unfortunately, it’s a principle often ignored.

For Athol Foden of naming consultancy Brighter Naming, the most prominent unpleasant brand name of recent quarters is Grok, the chatbot of Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Foden hates it so much he devoted an entire essay to what’s wrong with it.

“I still want to throw up when you say that name… and it is even worse in foreign languages,” he said in an interview. In his essay he called the brand a cross between “a suppressed swear word and a throat condition your doctor would prescribe antibiotics for.”

It’s not an anti-Musk stance. Foden is a fan of the entrepreneur’s Starlink as a name choice for the global satellite Internet service. It’s memorable and evocative in a positive way.

For other examples, we didn’t want to pick on current startups for their naming choices. So we looked instead to archives of startups past for other cases of harsh naming choices that didn’t pan out or are no longer operating under that brand.

Our shortlist included Quibi, a heavily funded short video startup with famous founders and a famously short shelf life. Others that have either folded or no longer operate under the original brand include Doostang, Gtrot, and Xobni (inbox spelled backwards, but not terribly clear how to pronounce.)

Another naming tactic to avoid is selecting a brand that evokes negative imagery or connotations.

“We always say: This is something you should be proud to wear on a hoodie,” said Bruno Benedini, co-founder of branding consultancy Taillight. If not, then reconsider.

Following this notion, one recently funded company name that rubbed both Benedini and your author the wrong way is Warhound, a startup focused on breeding dogs for roles in the military, law enforcement and emergency response that recently raised $200 million.

Sure, it’s memorable. But it sets an awfully aggressive tone, especially for a pet-pampering culture in which other startups promote offerings like dog spas, canine couture, and custom meals. While there’s a role for well-treated service dogs, it’s preferably far from any battlefield.

Or, as Benedini put it, “I’d be embarrassed to have Warhound on my hoodie.”

For other examples of less-than-stellar naming picks, we looked through the archives of startups past. One dud was Flud, which combines awkward spelling and imagery of a natural disaster. Boo.com, a defunct fashion site that was the iconic flops of the dot-com era also comes to mind, evoking fright more than the desire to shop. Another popular but questionable pick is Fire (sometimes alternately spelled Fyre), the chosen name of at least a dozen entries in the Crunchbase dataset.

It may still be in vogue to give your company a one-word name followed by AI. But don’t try to get a branding consultant to sign off on it.

Both Foden and Benedini advise against adding AI to the company name for multiple reasons. One is that it will likely sound dated going forward. Another criticism is that since virtually every startup incorporates AI to some extent, adopting a name with “AI” isn’t particularly meaningful.

If one does insist on an AI name, the minimum next step is to make sure it still works with those two letters on the end. Lots of companies — including Amazon (formerly Amazon.com) and Apple (initially Apple Computer) — have altered their names to keep up with the times and done just fine.

Despite all the advice on how to avoid an awful name, a part of me can’t help hoping more startups will just ignore it all. Then we could live in a world where startups sought funding with names like “Gruesome Grok AI” or “Festering Boil Labs.”

That said, there’s a reason startup naming is a serious endeavor, and bad choices often have equally bad consequences.

#5275. Bitwise XRP ETF Averages $14 Million in Daily Trading in Year One

The Bitwise XRP ETF traded an average of about $14 million a day over its first year on the market, resulting in over $3.5 billion in total trading volume, according to Bitwise.

In a post on X commemorating the Bitwise XRP ETF's first anniversary, Bitwise said the fund had recorded over $667 million in net inflows and had more than $376 million in assets under management (AUM) since launch.

Bitwise's XRP ETF started trading on Nov. 20, 2025, on NYSE Arca. It trades under the same ticker as the cryptocurrency it holds, XRP.

Investors can use the ETF's shares to track the price of the token through their brokerage accounts. The fund holds the XRP on behalf of investors. At launch, the ETF charged a 0.34% annual management fee. It also offered a fee waiver for the first $500 million in assets for the first month.

The $3.5 billion in trading volume is the total value of purchases and sales of the ETF's shares. This means the same ETF shares could trade repeatedly. If an investor sells their shares to another investor, that transaction increases trading volume. But the total XRP held in the fund doesn't change in that case.

On the other hand, the $667 million in net inflows represents the total dollar value of new shares issued over the past year minus redeemed shares.

AUM represents the total dollar value of a fund's assets at a specific moment. Since the fund's total assets are valued in dollars, AUM can fall below cumulative net inflows if the price of XRP declines, even as investors continue to put money into the fund.

The quarterly report filed by Bitwise with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) shows the impact of investor demand and XRP's price on the fund over the past year.

The net asset value of the fund increased from $299.1 million at the end of June to $614.9 million at the end of September.

Over $315.7 million was added to the fund's net assets during that quarter. Just over half of that $315.7 million came from new share creations.

The fund issued new shares with a total dollar value of $210.7 million. It also redeemed $32.8 million in shares during that quarter. So that left about $178 million in net new creations.

The fund issued 13.75 million shares and redeemed 2.42 million shares.

Coinbase CEO Brian Armstrong said on X that the company is repurchasing stock in the fourth quarter because investors are overlooking the potential of the payments business for AI agents.

"Good to take advantage of market dislocations," said Armstrong.

The company is buying back stock using funds previously authorized for repurchases. He didn't specify the number of COIN shares, the price or the amount spent.

At the start of the quarter, Coinbase had $1.96 billion left to repurchase stock. Over the prior three months, it repurchased 37,995 shares for a total cost of $5.3 million, at an average price of $139.91. All repurchases occurred in August, according to its third-quarter report.

Coinbase's board of directors initially authorized stock buybacks of up to $1 billion in October 2024. A year later, the buyback authorization was doubled. The company also received an option to repurchase some outstanding debt.

The board increased the buyback limit again in January 2026, bringing the total authorization to $4 billion.

Some buybacks have been carried out to cancel stock issued as employee compensation. By the end of September, the company had repurchased 10.2 million Class A shares and canceled more than 85% of the stock issued for employee compensation since the fourth quarter of 2024. This is according to an earnings presentation.

Armstrong envisions a scenario where crypto and AI are involved in different aspects of the same transaction.

For example, AI agents might help users make financial decisions and follow their instructions. Then, a crypto network may be used to transfer funds.

Coinbase wants to provide accounts, payment services, and marketplaces for humans and AI agents to use.

Now Armstrong is inviting developers to add their specialized AI models to Agentic.Market.

According to Armstrong, an AI agent can choose which specialist to hire for a task based on its capabilities and price. Coinbase provides the platform where agents can find specialists and pay them.

#5271. Hank Green is self-funding ClockwiseTV, a curated educational video platform for kids

“I was recently on a podcast and the host asked me what my lowest part of my career was,” Hank Green mused on a recent episode of his own podcast, Dear Hank & John.

That’s a tough question for anyone to answer, let alone someone who has spent about two decades regularly posting videos online for an increasingly broad audience.

“Really the low — the long low — was just watching as [the internet] went from being this lovely thing that a bunch of creatives were goofing around [on] to it being freaking everything, and mattering so much, and getting taken over by all tons of terrible vibes and algorithms selecting for outrage, and it being a huge degradation to the social order,” Green said.

That’s bleak, but Green is at least trying to lead by example in showing that we don’t have to accept that the good parts of the internet are gone forever. The notoriously entrepreneurial vlogbrother has spun up a new company with Leslie Morgan: ClockwiseTV, a curated, ad-free educational video platform for children ages 8 to 12.

“[Hank] came to me last September like, ‘I have had this idea for a really long time, and it stems from the fact that my child, who’s nine, always is asking me for five more minutes on whatever device he’s on,’” Morgan, who has spent 20 years working on the business side of the creator economy, told TechCrunch. “I was like, I have that same problem… ‘How do you contain time, but also give the child agency?’”

Clockwise’s answer to that question seems to be this: At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two 10-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left.

The startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad. According to a 2025 study by the Pew Research Center, about 51% of parents of children 12 or younger say their kid watches YouTube every day, among other video apps.

YouTube has a dedicated app for children under 13, YouTube Kids, which offers a wide range of parental controls, but the app can reportedly still serve children a wealth of low-quality AI slop. Other apps that don’t have a kids’ version can be even worse.

Clockwise says it is also solving that problem by hand-curating a library of educational videos from creators like Odd Animal Specimens, Draw with Jazza, and Nerdforge, as well as channels Green had a hand in creating, like Crash Course Kids and SciShow Kids.

“When you go into the app, there’s a dozen choices [of videos] that you can choose from to start,” Morgan, the startup’s CEO, said. “There’s search functionality as well, so you can say, ‘Hey, I’m really interested in math today,’ so you can look up Stand-up Maths and look at what’s available in that time frame.”

Some of these creators cater to people of all ages, but Clockwise says its team manually reviews each video it uploads and edits it so that it’s ready for younger eyes. The team might remove anything from embedded product placement to what Morgan calls “spectacle power tool use.”

“Simone Giertz, who’s a maker creator, tends to curse a lot. But a lot of that content is great for kids,” Morgan explains. “She makes a skateboard for her three-legged dog, and if she drops an f-bomb, we’re going to cut it out so that it’s suitable for children.”

Clockwise pays these creators an upfront fee to use their videos, then shares 25% of revenue based on watch time. Clockwise charges parents $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year to access the platform, which it promises will remain free of ads.

“Humans are checking [the videos] four times at least before it’s ever published into our app […] That will always stay,” Morgan said. “We’re not interested in using AI to wash down our content.”

So far, a few hundred parents have tested Clockwise with their children in beta. On Tuesday, the platform is opening to the public with apps made for iOS and Android smartphones and tablets.

The platform has not taken on any outside funding, and is funded by Green himself.

“It was really important that he had full control,” Morgan said. “He wanted to invest his own wealth into this. That was also really important because it is something he just believes in so wholeheartedly, as do I.”

#5270. Science Corporation’s brain tech is worth $3.5 billion after new funding

Science Corporation, the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the company said in a blog post.

Investors in the new round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage new technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

Science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for new conditions.

Hodak announced that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

With the funding, the company aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.

Still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The company is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

#5269. XRP Ledger Bug That Makes Trading Orders Disappear Is Addressed

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Official XRP Ledger's repository account received a proposed fix to keep only transaction-independent offer removals after a tec that should address the disappearance of failed transactions.

This particular change addresses a bug with order-book behavior around “tec” failures, which are failures where the transaction processing is rolled back. In some circumstances, offers can be removed when a "tec" failure occurs, even though the transaction that triggered it never succeeded.

In one scenario, a trader could have an existing offer removed before they’re able to add a replacement (for instance, if they don’t have enough reserve to add a new offer). In another, a more complicated Flow could temporarily leave an offer unfunded, only to have funds restored if a subsequent step fails, again resulting in an offer being removed even though the transaction that triggered it failed.

To address this issue, rippled will attempt to remove offers that were marked for removal upon tec failure any time a tec failure occurs. Previously, this was attempted for certain tec error codes but not others, with some additional restrictions around Flow-related offer removals (an offer will only be marked for removal if the owner’s balance has not changed in any relevant ways during the course of the Flow).

Offers that have already expired can still be removed, but offers owned by the transactor will be skipped. This is a best effort to make sure offers are consistently added/removed from the order book and should reduce confusing trade results.

Offers to/from regular XRP accounts and balances, XRP sends are unaffected and there are no proposed API changes.

This does not change XRP supply, fees, transaction capacity, etc. and is unlikely to have any effect on XRPL usage or XRP price (other than maybe making XRPL trading more appealing to traders).

This change would mostly affect traders using decentralized exchanges (DEXs) and particularly those using complex/routed/fill-or-kill orders/self-crosses.

On November 23, XRP briefly hit $1.026 before dropping below $1. Reports indicate crypto selling in general and ETF outflows have been putting pressure on XRP lately. By November 25, XRP was trading at ~$0.92. This software change would not be a catalyst for a price recovery of XRP.

#5268. Pedestal AI raises $4.7 million to agentify the supply chain

Delivery supply chains are the lifeblood of contemporary businesses — and a new startup is betting that purpose-built AI agents can make them run a lot more smoothly.

On Tuesday, Pedestal AI emerged from stealth with $4.7 million in seed funding. The company’s goal is to use agentic AI to make supply chains faster and more reliable — a plan that’s already brought them together with Fortune 500 companies and some of the largest shipping firms in the world.

The seed round was led by Eclipse, with participation from RRE, Converge VC, Timescale Ventures, and VitalStage. Pedestal says the funding will be used to expand its product and engineering time, grow the marketing organization, and support additional deployments.

In practice, much of Pedestal’s work is about removing friction from the shipping process — with agentic technology used as a means to that end. In one case, the company reduced missed deliveries for a major furniture company by 20% by deploying agents to take on some of the work that drivers were supposed to do. The agentic system they built would call customers 30 minutes before a delivery and collect any special instructions; if the call didn’t go through, a text would be sent from a separate system. Along the way, the deployment collected a wealth of data about friction points in the process, which could be used to optimize the system even further.

CEO Raj Aggarwal says contemporary AI systems are particularly useful for dealing with that data. “The challenge is that the data is messy and it’s constantly changing,” Aggarwal told TechCrunch. “It’s disparate because it sits in so many legacy systems. That’s what makes it hard.”

Supply chain AI has become a particularly hot space in recent months as alumni from autonomous driving teams look to launch their own startups. The supply chain startup Atomic, launched by a team of Tesla alumni, came out of stealth in 2025 with an emphasis on streamlining inventory. Another venture called Loop was launched by Uber alums to focus on predictive analytics.

As Aggarwal sees it, deliveries are particularly well-suited to training reinforcement learning systems. Because of their high volumes and easily measured outcomes, it’s easy to fine-tune contemporary AI systems toward what’s working and away from what isn’t.

Perhaps most importantly, it’s the kind of problem that can have an immediate effect on a client’s bottom line, making it easy to justify the expense.

“If you can get it right,” he told TechCrunch, “you can have really big impact.”

Dogecoin co-founder Billy Markus, who is known on X as Shibetoshi Nakamoto, has explained why, in his opinion, no one can predict the prices of cryptocurrencies.

Markus shared his opinion on Wednesday in a reply to an X post with a prediction that the price of Zcash (ZEC) would fall to $100.

"my opinion is that every single cryptocurrency has an arbitrary value mostly unrelated to anything except that people believe they can make more money if others buy it from them in the future and thus all future projections are pissing in the wind," the Dogecoin co-founder wrote.

Markus did not mention Zcash or any other token by name in his reply, and his post was about every single cryptocurrency on the market, including the one he created himself.

my opinion is that every single cryptocurrency has an arbitrary value mostly unrelated to anything except people believe they can make more money if others buy it from them in the future and thus all future projections are pissing in the wind

At the time of the post, ZEC was trading at around $728, up by 41.3% over the past year, according to price data on X.

The latest comment from Markus comes a week after Bitwise filed an S-1 registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission for a spot Zcash ETF. According to the filing, the fund is set to trade on the Texas Stock Exchange under the ticker ZEC, and it will not stake ZEC or use shielded transactions.

Markus created Dogecoin together with Jackson Palmer in December 2013. The two developers based the cryptocurrency on the Doge meme with a Shiba Inu dog, and they launched it as a joke about the crypto market of that time.

Markus has said in the past that it took him a couple of hours to write the code of Dogecoin. In 2021, Markus also said on X that he had sold all of his DOGE in 2015 after he lost his job, and that he got about the price of a used Honda Civic for it.

Since then, Markus has stayed active on X under the Shibetoshi Nakamoto name, and he often replies to posts about crypto prices, forecasts and new tokens.

In June 2022, Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates spoke about crypto and NFTs at the TechCrunch Sessions: Climate conference.

"As an asset class, it's 100% based on the greater fool theory — that somebody's going to pay more for it than I do," Gates said.

Earlier, at the Berkshire Hathaway annual meeting in April 2022, Warren Buffett said that he would not buy all of the Bitcoin in the world even for $25.

"If you told me you own all of the bitcoin in the world and you offered it to me for $25, I wouldn't take it because what would I do with it?" Buffett said.

According to Buffett, Bitcoin does not produce anything. At the same meeting, Buffett compared it with farmland and apartment buildings, and he said that he would pay for a share of them because farmland produces food and apartments produce rent.

#5266. Exchange Ledgers in the Middle as CFTC and SEC Diverge on What “Delivery” Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

A customer buys a token on a U.S. exchange and the app shows the balance. Under the CFTC's December 14 framework, nothing has been delivered yet.

Under the SEC's crypto proposal, delivery doesn't decide the question at all. An October 27 comment letter asks the two agencies to settle on one answer.

Open almost any crypto exchange app after a purchase and you'll see a clean number: 1.0000 ETH, available. To the customer, the asset is theirs. To the exchange's database, it's a row in an internal ledger. To federal regulators, that row is now being judged by two different tests that don't agree on what it means.

The Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) has opened an advance notice of proposed rulemaking on what it calls Regulation Crypto Asset Transactions (CTX) and Regulation Crypto Asset Markets (CAM). It sets out the agency's first formal view of "actual delivery" for crypto since it withdrew its 2020 guidance last December. Comments close on December 14.

The Securities and Exchange Commission's Regulation Crypto Assets proposal takes a different view of the same moment. Then, on October 27, a comment letter on the SEC's file raised the gap directly. It described the situation as "two conflicting definitions of the same physical facts" and asked the agencies to "please coordinate the definitions."

Delivery matters because it decides which rulebook applies.

For the CFTC, the answer comes from Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act. A leveraged, margined or financed retail commodity trade is treated like a futures contract unless "actual delivery" happens within 28 days. If delivery happens in time, the trade falls outside futures rules. If it doesn't, the exchange is effectively running a futures venue.

For the SEC, the question is whether a token is still part of an investment contract. Under the August proposal, a covered investment contract ends when the issuer has finished or permanently stopped its essential managerial efforts and files a Form TR transition report. Whether the buyer has received the token is not part of that test.

So one agency treats delivery as the deciding question, and the other barely considers it.

The CFTC's position is still preliminary, but it is detailed. Published in the Federal Register on October 13, the notice relies on the Monex case standard: actual delivery requires "the transfer of some meaningful degree of possession or control."

For crypto, the agency suggests that possession and control "may require possession of the credentials (e.g., private key(s))." It takes three positions that matter most to exchanges:

The agency is also asking whether control has to be exclusive, whether delivery can happen while a lien or security interest is outstanding, and how financing offered in an exchange's standard account documents affects whether a trade is covered at all.

The SEC's proposal, released on August 18, deals with a different question. It creates offering exemptions, including a $5 million startup exemption over four years, and a safe harbor for when a crypto asset's investment contract ends. Neither depends on where the token sits.

Under the proposal, a token held in a customer's self-custody wallet and a token recorded on an exchange's books are treated the same way. In both cases, the investment contract question depends on the issuer's managerial efforts and its filings.

That is the gap the October 27 letter tries to close. Its author, who describes themselves as a fintech founder designing a consumer platform, argues that "where the customer holds the private keys or execution is on-chain, with custody evidence, the asset should be treated as delivered and the covered-investment-contract analysis should end there."

Running four common exchange transactions through both frameworks shows where the tests split.

Trade one: a fully paid purchase left on the exchange.

Trade two: the same purchase withdrawn to a self-custody wallet on day three.

Trade three: a margined purchase kept on the exchange's ledger for 30 days.

Trade four: an on-chain swap that settles directly into the user's wallet.

The pattern is consistent. Self-custody is the only position that clearly counts as delivery under the CFTC's view and also ends the analysis under the letter's proposed SEC fix. Everything left on an exchange's internal ledger stays in an unclear position. The CFTC treats it as undelivered and the SEC's text doesn't address it.

The letter was filed on October 27, a week after the SEC's October 20 comment deadline. It is anonymous and brief, but its main concern is practical. If the definitions stay separate, it warns, founders will have to design products around whichever rule is stricter.

It is the only filing on either docket so far that sets the two definitions side by side.

The CFTC process is still at the advance-notice stage, so a formal proposal will follow. For U.S. platforms, though, the direction is clear. Under the CFTC's preliminary reading, an exchange that keeps customer assets in internal ledger accounts has not delivered them. If that exchange also offers margin or financing, it is on track to be treated as a futures venue.

The SEC's final rule could adopt the letter's custody-based approach or keep delivery out of its analysis entirely. Until one of those happens, the same ledger entry can be undelivered for one regulator and irrelevant for the other.

Exchanges and their customers have until December 14 to say which definition should prevail. The real decision is whether "delivered" ends up meaning the same thing at both agencies.

#5265. Nvidia’s startup stakes ballooned to $65B, but Huang’s exit puts future deals in doubt

Nvidia’s equity in private companies continues to grow: It revealed its stakes are now worth $65.5 billion on Tuesday, up from the $22 billion reported in January. The increase includes both new investments and significant markups of existing portfolio companies.

The company invested $16 billion into equities in the past quarter alone, it said, and $58 billion in the past nine months of its fiscal year. This amount includes buying shares in public and private companies, yet it shows how the chipmaker made massive bets over the course of the year, especially compared to last year; in November 2025, the company reported spending $5 billion buying equity in the first nine months of that fiscal year.

But it’s unclear if this growth will continue under the interim CEO and Jensen Huang’s successor.

Nvidia stated in late 2023 that the goal of its corporate investing is to expand the AI ecosystem by backing startups it considers to be “game changers and market makers.”  Over the nearly three years that followed, the chipmaker has invested in nearly 350 startups, according to PitchBook. The companies Nvidia backed include Anthropic and OpenAI; neolabs like Thinking Machines and Reflection; neoclouds, like Lambda, Nscale, and Crusoe; as well as other companies developing AI infrastructure, robotics startups, and applications.

It’s also become a big financier of the data center build-out, reporting $118 billion in guarantees with $105 billion of that the backstop it supplied for OpenAI’s $500 billion data center in Ohio.

The company made those commitments by allocating a meaningful portion of its excess cash flows. In Tuesday’s earnings call, Kress said Nvidia would continue providing financing assistance to strong customers and that “as the market matures and additional sources of capital become available,” the company would be “rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”

But the question for the VC ecosystem is whether the company will continue to back startups at anywhere near the same level without Huang at the helm.

Huang’s rampant dealmaking has reportedly been a source of concern for Kress. Investors have told TechCrunch that they anticipate she will take a more conservative approach to startup investing, becoming more selective with new investments and writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio companies.

“We intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders during this last quarter and going forward,” Kress said on the earnings call on Tuesday. Just how strategic startups will be under her leadership, and under the future permanent CEO, remains to be seen. But for now, VCs are bracing for a meaningful pullback in capital.

#5264. Bitcoin (BTC) For $99,000? Bitcoin Refraction Model Puts a "Fair" Price

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Bitcoin's long-term trend value, based on various models like "Plan B", has been set ridiculously high, so chasing targets set by those models might not be the best decision out there, considering modern market conditions.

A revised Bitcoin Power Law model sets BTC's long-term price at $99,000, which is almost $50,000 below the $146,725 estimate that has been used by the traditional Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) model.

The creator of the newer, accordingly more accurate model believes the Bitcoin Power Law is still valid, but the fair value is certainly nowhere near the relevant market conditions.

One way or another, the newer models still set the current price threshold at one of the lowest historical levels in the history of the asset—approximately the 1st percentile of its distribution, which means that it stands among 60 of Bitcoin's daily closes that fell below this threshold.

The new model uses a completely different method for calculation: Quantile Regression instead of Ordinary Least Squares (OLS). The main difference is that OLS guesses Bitcoin's price trend based on its historical averages, while QR uses specific points in the price distribution, not an average. Essentially, the newer calculation model smoothens out extremes that made OLS less accurate.

Despite the newer calculation and estimation approach, the improved calculation algorithm and everything else, models are estimating, not making solid predictions.

There are thousands of other factors to consider when determining Bitcoin's next move, so any kind of model is useful only for evaluating the momentum and historical significance of the most recent movements.

The model also places its 0.1 percentile at $55,185, a level below which Bitcoin has closed only six times. The creator argues that only the lower part of Bitcoin's price distribution, between the 0.1 and 5th percentiles, may continue following the Power Law, while higher levels gradually move down towards this lower boundary.

The model also uses Protocol Time instead of Calendar Time. Still, its creator maintains that the Power Law is not broken. The problem, according to this view, is how previous models measured it and how much they allowed market bubbles to influence the results.

Traders on Polymarket now see about a 97% chance that the Fed raises rates at its December 8-9 meeting. That would be the Fed’s second hike of 2026, after September’s.

So what does a December hike mean for crypto?

The Bureau of Economic Analysis report gave the Fed little reason to wait:

Strong incomes and sticky prices are the mix that worries a central bank. Polymarket’s December market puts a quarter-point hike at 94% and a half-point hike at 2.6%, with $58 million traded on it.

The year has turned around for the Fed. In January, two officials voted for a rate cut. By September, under Chair Kevin Warsh, who took over in May, the Fed raised its target range by 0.25 points to 3.75%-4%. In October, it held, but two officials wanted another hike. A December move would lift the range to 4%-4.25%.

The inflation report landed on a market already shaken by the AI sell-off. Early on Wednesday, CNBC’s market blog showed the Nasdaq down 4.4%, the S&P 500 down 3.1% and the Dow down more than 1,000 points.

Higher rates hit expensive growth stocks hardest, because they make future profits worth less today. Bitcoin, which has traded with tech stocks all autumn, fell more than 4% in 24 hours.

A hike sounds like bad news for crypto. This year’s data tell a more mixed story. We measured bitcoin’s move in the week after each 2026 Fed rate decision, from the open on decision day to the close seven days later.

The pattern fits an old market saying: sell the rumor, buy the news. By the time the Fed acts, a hike is often already in the price. Seven meetings and one hike is a small sample, so treat it as a clue, not a rule.

The December Fed rate decision is now about the size of the hike and what officials signal for 2027. Until then, $57,800 is the line to watch for bitcoin.

#5262. Clock Ticking on Zcash’s Sprout Pool: 22,263 ZEC Unmoved Ahead of NU7 Lock

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Daily pool data shows Sprout holders moved more than 300 ZEC out in a September rush, then almost stopped. The last withdrawal was on October 19.

Unless someone acts in the next few days, nearly all of what remains will be unspendable at block 3,543,405.

Most coverage of Zcash's upcoming Sprout freeze quotes the same figure, about 22,000 ZEC. That number is accurate, but it is a single snapshot. It doesn't show whether the people who own those coins are doing anything about the deadline.

We checked the pool every day, and the answer so far is no.

According to ZecStats' daily value-pool records, Sprout has held exactly 22,263.34162335 ZEC since October 19. That is 11 straight days, and more than 12,000 blocks, without a single zatoshi leaving the pool. Our October 25 piece recorded the drop from 22,309 ZEC to 22,263 ZEC. Since then the balance hasn't moved.

ZecStats publishes a daily CSV of every Zcash value pool, using the last block of each UTC day. Its figures follow the valuePools field that a full node returns through the getblockchaininfo call. The archive starts on July 30, 2026, and gives a 92-day picture of the Sprout pool.

Across those 92 days, about 374 ZEC, or 1.65% of the pool, left Sprout. That is an average of roughly 4 ZEC a day. The average hides the real pattern, though: the pool moved on only 15 of the 92 days.

Most of the withdrawals came in a few large transfers in September:

Together with smaller moves on August 31, September 17 and September 19, the 30 days to September 29 saw 310.5 ZEC leave Sprout. That is about 10 ZEC a day.

October was much quieter. Apart from one withdrawal of 46.05 ZEC on October 19, the month's activity was small change:

Since October 19, there has been no movement at all.

At September's pace, about 70 ZEC more would leave before activation. At October's pace, it would be well under 15 ZEC. On the last 11 days' pace, the answer is zero.

The deadline is set in ZIP 259, which defines how the NU7 network upgrade is deployed. It sets the mainnet activation height at 3,543,405.

NU7 does not introduce a new transaction format. Instead, after activation, version 4 transactions become invalid, while versions 5 and 6 remain valid. Sprout's design is the problem. As ZIP 259 puts it: "Because Sprout transfers can only be represented by version 4 transactions, funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The coins would not be destroyed, and NU7 does not change Zcash's supply cap. They would simply be stuck in a pool that no valid transaction can spend from. Today the stranded amount would be 22,263 ZEC, about 0.13% of the roughly 17.01 million ZEC in circulation.

ZIP 259 also skips Zcash's usual three-month gap between the first supporting software release and activation. Operators running unsupported software could stay online and follow a pre-NU7 chain.

As of ZecStats' latest update on October 30 at 13:09 UTC, the chain was at block 3,535,877. That leaves 7,528 blocks until activation.

In October, the network averaged about 1,147 blocks a day, or one roughly every 75.3 seconds. At that rate, block 3,543,405 arrives around 02:00–03:00 UTC on November 6. That is the evening of November 5 in the Americas and the early hours of November 6 in Europe and Africa.

Small changes in block times could move that window by a few hours. Holders who plan to move funds on the final day risk missing the cutoff.

In practice, getting funds out of Sprout means sending a version 4 transaction that moves them into a newer pool before activation. Users need software that can still build Sprout transactions and a synced node or wallet that recognizes their old notes.

The September withdrawals show that some holders are still paying attention. Several were round amounts, such as 99.998 ZEC, which is consistent with someone moving 100 ZEC and paying a fee. The 11-day pause since October 19 suggests something else: most of the remaining 22,263 ZEC may belong to keys that are lost, forgotten or no longer used.

That has been part of the debate about Sprout for years. A pool that has been shrinking slowly since Zcash's early days is now on a fixed timetable. The daily data indicates that most of its remaining balance is not being moved.

Every report that cites "about 22,000 ZEC at risk" is technically correct. The more useful figure for anyone tracking the upgrade is the rate of change, and right now that rate is zero.

The useful thing to watch over the next week is whether the Sprout line in ZecStats' daily data moves again before block 3,543,405. If it doesn't, Zcash will activate NU7 with about 22,263 ZEC permanently locked in its first shielded pool. That would be one of the largest deliberate freezes of user funds by any major blockchain upgrade, and nearly all of it would be coins whose owners did not move them in time.

#5261. India’s Humyn Labs raises $47M to feed US robotics companies the data they need

As demand grows for real-world data to train robots, India’s Humyn Labs has raised $47 million in Series A financing to help U.S. AI and robotics companies build models that can operate in physical environments.

The funding comprises $26 million in equity led by Accel, with participation from Prosus Ventures, BeeGlobal, Bajaj Finance’s Finserv Intelligence and Bajaj Alts AI Opportunities Fund, Dallas Venture Capital, Lighthouse Canton, and Jump Trading. It also includes $21 million in venture debt led by Lighthouse Canton, with participation from Trifecta Capital.

Companies around the world are trying to build robots capable of performing everyday human tasks, but getting enough quality data to train them remains difficult. Startups, including Mecka AI, XDOF, and MicroAGI, are already tackling the problem by collecting real-world data for robotics training. Bengaluru-based Humyn Labs aims to compete with them.

Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which means tagging what happens in each clip so AI can learn from it. The startup collects data across over 20 countries in Latin America and Asia, with Brazil, India, and South Korea serving as its main hubs, co-founder Manish Agarwal (pictured above, right) said in an interview.

Agarwal, the former CEO of Indian gaming company Nazara Technologies, founded Humyn Labs in February with Ishank Gupta (pictured above, left), a former executive at the brewing giant AB InBev. The duo previously founded Kratos Studios, now known as KGeN. KGeN has a network of contributors across emerging markets, and that network helps Humyn Labs collect data in people’s homes, the founders told TechCrunch.

Collecting footage of human activity is only part of the challenge, Agarwal said. He added that Humyn Labs also uses software to track hand movements, interactions with objects, and other details, turning raw recordings into data that AI models can learn from.

“Scale, diversity, and quality are important aspects, and they need to work in tandem,” Agarwal said.

Humyn Labs says it has 12 paying customers, including frontier AI labs, robotics companies, and developers of world models. About 90% of its revenue comes from the U.S., Gupta said, though he declined to name specific customers.

The startup generated $10 million in revenue between April and October and has another $20 million in signed contracts, Agarwal told TechCrunch, adding that a further $20 million in deals has yet to be finalized.

That growth has also increased Humyn Labs’ need for working capital, Agarwal said, explaining the $21 million venture debt component. The startup pays workers and data collection partners daily or weekly but typically waits 30 to 60 days to receive payments from its AI lab customers. Borrowing helps bridge that gap and is less dilutive than selling more equity, he said.

Agarwal said Humyn Labs collects data from people doing their usual work or household chores instead of asking them to perform staged activities. The startup works with local partners to identify collection sites and oversee the process. “The worker is a worker who is incentivized, but he needs to be monitored and supervised for the right input,” he stated.

Humyn Labs currently has 51 full-time employees, most based in Bengaluru, plus a network of local partners across the countries where it collects data, Agarwal said.

Will Crypto Recover? Everyone is wondering this right now after the entire crypto market surged around +2% overnight. An Optimistic Look After Bitcoin’s Rebound Above $ 60,000.

The cryptocurrency market delivered a welcome dose of relief over the past 24 hours. Bitcoin reclaimed the $60,000 level, rising roughly 2.5–3.5% to trade between $60,400 and $60,800, while the broader market advanced in tandem.

Ethereum climbed to the $1,690–$1,710 range, XRP advanced toward $0.95–$0.96, and total crypto market capitalization pushed higher toward $2.15–$2.16 trillion.

After weeks of heavy selling and extreme fear, the bounce has sparked renewed discussion about whether this could mark the early stages of a more sustained recovery heading into 2027.

Prices became deeply oversold after Bitcoin’s slide toward the mid-$50,000s earlier in the week, with short-term RSI readings hitting extreme lows that historically attract dip-buyers and mean-reversion algorithms.

Forced short covering amplified the move higher as leveraged bearish positions were liquidated. A concurrent recovery in technology and AI-related equities improved broader risk appetite, and crypto’s high correlation with those sectors helped lift digital assets.

Thin holiday trading volumes around Thanksgiving also magnified price swings. On the policy front, progress on a U.S. Strategic Bitcoin Reserve bill that cleared a House committee provided a modest sentiment boost, reminding participants that longer-term institutional and governmental interest has not vanished.

Its ability to hold above $60,000 after testing lower support is constructive in the short term. While November has seen record ETF outflows exceeding $5 billion, the latest rebound shows that demand can still emerge at discounted levels.

Ethereum has tracked Bitcoin closely, benefiting from improved risk appetite and its role as the leading smart-contract platform. XRP has shown relative strength in the bounce, gaining around 3–4.5% as traders watch for potential follow-through if it can challenge higher levels near $1.

Looking further ahead, the case for recovery into 2027 rests on several structural factors. Crypto markets have repeatedly shown resilience after deep corrections, often bottoming when sentiment reaches extreme fear, as in recent weeks.

Persistent institutional infrastructure, including spot ETFs, corporate treasury strategies, and ongoing development in tokenization and payments, provides a foundation for renewed capital inflows once macroeconomic conditions stabilize.

Policy developments, such as clearer regulatory frameworks or expanded strategic reserve discussions, could act as positive catalysts. One example is the US Bitcoin Strategic Reserve Bill, which was recently cleared and is now headed to the House.

Historically, post-halving cycles and periods of oversold conditions have preceded stronger multi-month advances, and many participants view current levels as a potential accumulation zone rather than the start of a prolonged bear market.

Of course, risks remain. Continued heavy ETF outflows, sticky inflation data, or a shift toward tighter monetary policy could pressure prices again.

Yet the speed with which buyers stepped in during the latest dip suggests underlying demand remains. If Bitcoin can build a series of higher lows and reclaim key moving averages, confidence is likely to improve across the board.

In short, while one rebound does not confirm a full bull market, the past 24 hours offer encouraging signs that selling pressure may be exhausting itself.

Combined with oversold technicals, short covering, supportive equity moves, and longer-term policy and institutional tailwinds, crypto has a credible path to recover more meaningfully through the remainder of 2026 and into 2027.

For now, the market has shown it can still bounce, and that alone is a constructive first step. However, green weekly closes across the major cap tokens are the next step in seeing whether this rally has any legs.

#5259. Ripple Custody Partners With Major Private Bank in Türkiye

Ripple has once again landed a major partnership in Türkiye, but this time around with one of the country’s largest private banks, putting XRP in the spotlight.

While this comes as part of Ripple’s growing expansion into the traditional financial space, the blockchain firm announced it has partnered with Yapı Kredi, a major Turkish private bank, to support its cryptocurrency business.

As part of the partnership agreement, Ripple Custody will help the bank to securely manage its digital assets and provide custody services for its crypto trading platform dubbed Yapı Kredi Kripto.

While the partnership demands the full integration of the Ripple custodial infrastructure, the firm revealed that Ripple Custody will be installed on the bank's own premises.

This way, Yapı Kredi will have access to adequate security and control it needs to manage all digital assets on behalf of its customers, boosting its security.

The development is significant for the bank and the broader Turkish crypto market; it also marks a major milestone for Ripple as the firm claims to be the only custody service provider currently supporting leading Turkish banks licensed by the CMB as crypto asset custodians.

It is important to note that Türkiye currently stands as one of the world's top 10 retail crypto markets, with XRP recorded as one of its most widely used cryptocurrencies.

With Yapı Kredi now fortifying its position as a major player in Türkiye’s fast-growing crypto market, its partnership with the blockchain firm associated with XRP is likely to open new opportunities for XRP while positioning it for bigger adoption in the country.

#5258. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.
