#5196. How Bittensor's Gamma Turns Every AI Payment Into an Alpha Burn

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Paying a Bittensor subnet with gamma burns its alpha token. Here is how gamma gets minted, how the lower-price rule works and why the credit can never be converted back.Pay a Bittensor subnet for an AI answer with gamma, and your payment vanishes. The alpha token behind it gets burned, the credit gets spent, and nobody can redeem either one.

Using a subnet's service today usually means creating an account, adding funds and collecting an API key, and every additional subnet repeats the routine. Opentensor announced gamma to cut that friction. With gamma, a Bittensor wallet handles both access and payment across any subnet that adopts the standard.The mechanics are laid out in the gamma guide in the subtensor docs. Gamma is a credit a subnet can accept as payment, valued in US dollars. A customer gets it by burning that subnet's alpha token, and each dollar of burned alpha value mints one gamma, so a burn valued at $100 creates 100 gamma.Each balance stays tied to the subnet where it was created. Gamma minted for subnet 51 can't pay for a service on any other subnet. Root switches the system on network-wide, and each subnet owner or lease beneficiary then enables it for their own subnet.

Customers have two ways in. They can pay with TAO, and the protocol buys the subnet’s alpha and burns it in a single transaction. Or they can pay with alpha they already hold on that subnet, and the protocol burns it directly to create gamma.

Setup takes four steps. The customer creates a fresh hotkey that will act as an API key, associates it with their coldkey, looks up the service they want and mints. The docs give the command: btcli gamma mint --netuid 51 --hotkey API_KEY --amount-tao 10 --service-hotkey SERVICE_HOTKEY. The TAO route follows the same pool and flow accounting as stake-burn and creates no stake position. Users who hold stake can burn it with mint-gamma-with-stake, and --amount-alpha all burns the whole position.

The gamma lands in a deposit. Each deposit belongs to the minting coldkey and is keyed by the API-key hotkey, which signs the customer's requests. A hotkey holds at most one deposit per subnet, and a coldkey holds at most 64 per subnet. The docs warn against reusing a staking hotkey or a coldkey, because requests signed with the key get paid from the deposit.A few guardrails apply. A mint must reach at least 0.1 gamma. By default, the SDK quotes the mint first and fails it if the result lands more than 5% below the quote. The mint also needs a TAO/USD price no older than 300 blocks, about an hour.

Gamma’s valuation rule decides how much credit a burn buys. The protocol values the burned alpha in TAO, then converts that figure to dollars through an on-chain TAO/USD price feed. The TAO value equals alpha multiplied by the lower of two prices, the gamma price and the spot price, which the docs write as alpha × min(gamma price, spot price).

Every subnet keeps a gamma price. When a subnet registers, the price starts at the median alpha price across subnets. After that it moves asymmetrically. If spot falls, the gamma price falls to match at once. If spot rises, the gamma price climbs slowly toward it, closing a small slice of the gap each block, so the gap halves every 600 blocks, roughly two hours. However high spot jumps, the gamma price can at most double every 600 blocks.An example shows the effect. Say a user burns 100 alpha when spot sits at 0.05 TAO but the gamma price lags at 0.04. The mint uses 0.04, which gives 4 TAO of value, and at $400 per TAO that mints 1,600 gamma. Had the gamma price caught up, the same burn would mint 2,000, so the lag costs the burner 400 gamma. A short-lived pump buys no extra credit. The figures are illustrative, but the rule comes straight from the docs.The TAO/USD feed gets similar damping. A root-controlled oracle supplies the price, and the accepted price falls to a lower feed immediately but rises at most 66 parts per million per block, about 2% an hour. The docs admit the oracle is trusted: its accepted price can climb up to roughly 61% a day until root replaces or removes it.One more detail matters. The docs say alpha is valued at these prices, not at what selling it would return, so a burn that is large relative to the pool is worth more than a sale would be. A big burner gets credit for full value instead of a slipped sale price.Once minted, gamma holds its dollar value whether TAO or alpha prices rise or fall. Service providers still set their own prices.

To use a service, a person or an AI agent signs a request with a hotkey from their Bittensor wallet. The subnet owner, or another authorized account, deducts the required credits from that hotkey's gamma balance before delivering the service. Nothing transfers to anyone. The designated spender calls `spend-gamma` with up to 512 entries per call, each naming a hotkey, an amount and a 32-byte reference, and the spent gamma is destroyed on the spot.The reference doubles as a receipt. By convention it holds the service's own ID for the request being paid, returned with the response, so the customer can match each spend to a specific request. The chain repeats the reference in its events and reads it nowhere else, so an entry sent twice spends twice.Customers keep control throughout. The minting coldkey can set a daily spend cap that refills linearly over 7,200 blocks, about a day, and a cap of zero pauses the deposit. The coldkey can also change the spender, keep separate deposits for different apps and agents, and top up an existing deposit without switching hotkeys. Because the coldkey can pause or redirect at any moment, services spend ahead: they spend what they are about to serve, then serve what was spent. A spender can hand this right to a `GammaSpend` proxy, which can make no other call.Both minting and spending leave public records on-chain, so anyone can audit how much credit a subnet has created and how much customers have used.

The limits are strict. Gamma can't be transferred to another wallet, and it can't be converted back into alpha or TAO. It confers no claim on any party and can't be redeemed. Each subnet chooses whether, and at what prices, it accepts its own gamma.

The docs flag the sharpest risk directly: dissolving or pruning a subnet destroys all of its gamma, and holders receive nothing. A customer who prepaid a large deposit to a subnet that later shuts down loses it. Moving gamma between your own deposits is allowed, and a deposit opened under someone else's hotkey stays yours, since you can pull the gamma back at any time.A coldkey swap adds a few wrinkles. While one is announced, the coldkey's gamma calls are refused, though its spenders keep spending. After a subnet owner swaps coldkeys, deposits that name the old one keep it until the owner republishes its service.

The docs answer the economic question in one sentence: spent gamma pays its spender nothing. The value of the burned alpha accrues to the subnet's alpha holders.

That makes gamma a direct demand mechanism for alpha. Creating gamma always burns the subnet's alpha, which removes those tokens from circulation for good. When customers pay with TAO, the protocol first buys alpha from the subnet's pool, so TAO-funded purchases add buying pressure before the burn. Every dollar of AI usage ties a purchase of service credits to a burn of alpha.

A service operator earns through the alpha it holds and the emissions its subnet receives, not through a payment from customers. The structure rewards subnets that attract real usage, since usage shrinks their alpha supply.Two questions remain open. Customers get dollar-denominated credit, but the burn that funds it follows alpha prices, so heavy usage during a price spike may feel expensive. Holders also carry the dissolution risk, which will push careful buyers toward established subnets. Which services accept gamma, and at what price, will show whether this becomes a real payments layer or a niche tool. The mechanism is clear, and adoption is the unknown.

Shiba Inu (SHIB) met Thanksgiving Day with a "Bull" label on its four-hour price chart. The label appeared on the relative strength index (RSI) of the SHIB/USD chart on TradingView, and on Thursday afternoon SHIB was trading at around $0.00000364, up 1.4% on the day.

On Saturday, SHIB fell as low as $0.00000337, according to TradingView. It was the lowest price of SHIB since 2021, and before that, the lowest price of SHIB in 2026 was $0.00000411 at the July 17 close. On Wednesday, the token dropped close to the Saturday low again. According to the chart, the RSI was around 23 on Saturday and around 32 on Wednesday, and the "Bull" label appeared next to the Wednesday reading.

The Crypto Fear and Greed Index on CoinMarketCap showed 13 on Wednesday, up from 10 on Tuesday.

The four-hour SHIB chart also showed the label on Oct. 27 and Nov. 5. It appeared twice more between Nov. 17 and Nov. 19, and two days later SHIB fell to its Saturday low.

The daily SHIB chart had the same label in late June and in July. On Thursday, there was no new label on the daily chart.

SHIB has lost 22.7% in November so far, according to CryptoRank data as of Nov. 22. The token also lost 29.6% and 24.8% in November of 2021 and 2022, respectively. In November of 2023 and 2024, SHIB gained 6.62% and 48.8%, and last November it fell 16.2%.

SHIB's median December return is -17.6%, and its average December return is -11.4%, according to CryptoRank data. SHIB gained 24.6% in December 2023 and lost 21% and 17.6% in December of 2024 and 2025, respectively. In 2026, SHIB has lost value in six of 11 months so far. In July, August and September, the token gained 12.2%, 7.55% and 13.5%, respectively. SHIB lost 24% in June and 18.6% in October.

On Jan. 1, SHIB closed at $0.00000692, according to CoinGecko. SHIB set its record high of $0.00008845 on Oct. 28, 2021, and in December of that year it lost 29.5%, according to CryptoRank. In January 2022, the token lost another 36%.

The number of SHIB holders on Ethereum passed 1.7 million on Nov. 17, according to Etherscan. CryptoQuant data from that day showed about 312 billion SHIB leaving exchanges.

On Thursday, SHIB was No. 34 on CoinMarketCap with a market capitalization of $2.14 billion. Its circulating supply stood at 589.23 trillion SHIB. Bittensor (TAO) was one place higher, and its market capitalization was also $2.14 billion. Hedera (HBAR) was No. 31 at $2.37 billion, and the PayPal USD (PYUSD) stablecoin held the 32nd spot between them.

#5194. Bitcoin Price Could Crash to $39K Despite Slowing ETF Outflows: Is Worst Yet to Come?

ETF outflows are slowing, but historical cycles and the 0.786 Fibonacci level point to a potential BTC bottom between $39,000 and $44,000.

In Bitcoin news this week, the selling from US spot Bitcoin ETFs is easing, but the price has not followed. On Tuesday, November 24, the funds lost a net $232 million. That was less than half of Monday’s $570 million.

It was still the sixth day of outflows in a row. The funds have shed about $2.6 billion since November 17 and nearly $5 billion this month, led by BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT).

Bitcoin spot ETFs have recorded SIX consecutive trading sessions of net outflows, with approximately 41,540 BTC withdrawn over that period.

The latest session saw another 3,780 BTC leave the funds, bringing further pressure on institutional demand.

BlackRock's IBIT accounted… pic.twitter.com/PUKLdaUgKS

— CryptoSavingExpert ® (@CryptoSavingExp) November 25, 2026

Bitcoin keeps sliding anyway. It trades near $58,900 on Wednesday, down 53% from its October 2025 record of $126,272. On Saturday, it touched $55,081, its lowest price in more than two years.

So if the funds are selling less, where could Bitcoin’s bear market end? We checked where Bitcoin bottomed in every past cycle, using Fibonacci retracement levels, ratios traders use to measure how much of a rally gets erased.

SoSoValue’s ETF flow figures, as reported this week, show the pressure easing:

Even after the selling, the funds still hold about $52 billion of net inflows since launch. That is roughly 83% of their October 2025 peak, so most ETF buyers have not left.

For Bitcoin news readers, slower outflows don’t mean buyers are back, though. They mean less forced selling from one big source. For the price to turn, the flows need to flip to inflows.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best New Crypto to Hodl

Fibonacci retracements measure how much of a rally a market gives back. Traders watch a handful of ratios, mainly 0.618 and 0.786, as places where a drop may stop.

We measured each Bitcoin cycle on Bitstamp’s daily price history since 2011. Each runs from one bear-market bottom to the next record high. We then checked how much of that move was erased by the next bottom.

That is the less-reported Bitcoin news: each bear market stopped a little earlier than the last, by three to four points each time. If that trend holds, the next bottom would land near the 0.786 Fibonacci level, a 78.6% retracement.

This cycle runs from the 2022 low of $15,479 to the $126,272 record. On that range, 0.786 sits at about $39,200. So far, Bitcoin has given back 64.3%. Saturday’s low already cut through the 0.618 level at $57,800.

A log scale treats a doubling the same at any price. On that scale, past bottoms came at shallower ratios, rising from 33% to 48%. The 0.5 level on that scale for this cycle is about $44,200. Both methods point to a $39,000 to $44,000 zone.

EXPLORE: BTC Price Drops 15% as Gold and Silver Dump: Can December’s Fed Decision Turn It?

Bitcoin trades at $58,930 on Binance, below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $71,954, and its 200-day EMA at $74,702.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best Low-Cap Crypto

The Bitcoin news to watch is the ETF flow data. A first day of inflows would be the clearest sign the selling is done. Until then, past cycles say the bottom could still be well below today’s price.

Bitcoin (BTC) has returned to a critical price zone after failing to sustain its recovery above $80,000. Following the recent sell-off across global markets, BTC has dropped toward $63,000, bringing an important support level back into focus. The decline comes amid weakening demand for risk assets, heavy liquidations in leveraged positions and growing uncertainty surrounding institutional participation.

The bigger question is whether Bitcoin can sustain above $60K or face another correction toward $52K. With $65K, $70K and $81K emerging as important recovery levels, this Bitcoin price prediction examines the updated technical structure and outlook through 2026 and beyond. This Bitcoin price prediction breaks down the technical structure, key catalysts and potential BTC targets through 2026, 2030 and beyond.

Bitcoin is approaching December near $61,000, with its broader market structure remaining under pressure after the recent correction. The failure to reclaim higher price levels, continued weakness in spot Bitcoin ETF flows and uncertainty surrounding the Federal Reserve’s December policy decision could limit recovery attempts. The immediate support zone sits around $58,000–$60,000, followed by stronger downside support near $53,000–$55,000. A sustained breakdown below $58,000 could increase the likelihood of another test of the lower support region.

On the upside, Bitcoin needs to reclaim $62,000–$65,000 to establish a more convincing recovery. A breakout above $65,000 could open the way toward $68,000–$70,000, although stronger institutional demand would likely be needed to sustain that move. Considering the current selling pressure, BTC could remain volatile through December, with a cautious outlook unless buyers regain control above $65,000.

Bitcoin’s 2026 outlook has turned increasingly cautious following its correction toward $60,000, leaving the cryptocurrency nearly 49% below its October 2025 all-time high. The daily technical structure remains bearish, with BTC trading below its 50-day and 200-day moving averages near $79,400 and $72,900, respectively. The $60,000–$62,000 region is an important downside support zone, while reclaiming $70,000–$73,000 would offer the first meaningful sign of recovery. Stronger institutional demand and improving liquidity could help Bitcoin approach $80,000–$90,000 by year-end. However, continued selling pressure could push BTC toward $50,000–$55,000.

Bitcoin’s year-end recovery depends on whether buyers can defend the $60,000 support region and reclaim the $70,000–$73,000 resistance band. A sustained breakout could improve the bullish case, while a breakdown below $60,000 would increase downside risks.

Bitcoin’s on-chain structure is strengthening as the price recovers toward $85,000, with two signals pointing to a tighter supply environment. Exchange reserves have fallen to 2.68 million BTC, the lowest level shown on the supplied chart since at least September 2023. More importantly, reserves have continued declining across multiple price cycles, suggesting that the reduction in exchange-held supply is not simply a short-term reaction to price movements.

At the same time, short-term holders have rebuilt a $43.8 billion unrealized profit cushion, with STH market capitalization at $333.9 billion versus $290.1 billion in realized capitalization. That puts the cohort roughly 15% above its realized value, reversing the unrealized-loss position seen when Bitcoin traded closer to $60,000. The recovery indicates that recent buyers are back in aggregate profit as BTC approaches $85,000.

Taken together, the data presents a constructive on-chain backdrop: exchange-held supply is shrinking while short-term holder profitability is recovering. The key question for the next phase is whether reserves continue falling as BTC moves higher, or whether a stronger rally encourages previously withdrawn coins to return to exchanges and increases available selling supply.

KuCoin will delist Monero (XMR) on Nov. 30, the exchange announced on Thursday. XMR dropped as low as $436 after the announcement and lost almost 15% within four hours, according to Kraken data on TradingView.

In the notice, KuCoin said that XMR would be delisted "in accordance with the Special Treatment Rules of KuCoin." The exchange closed XMR deposits on Thursday and will remove the XMR/USDT, XMR/USDC, XMR/ETH and XMR/BTC pairs at 08:00 UTC on Nov. 30.

KuCoin will also shut down XMR trading bots, Convert swaps and Earn products before the delisting. Users can withdraw XMR until Dec. 31, and KuCoin said that it could close withdrawals earlier if the Monero network stops producing blocks or processing transfers.

On Thursday, KuCoin's XMR/USDT pair had $73.8 million in 24-hour volume, according to CoinMarketCap. It was the largest Monero spot market and accounted for 47% of XMR spot trading. HTX's XMR/USDT pair was second with $29.5 million.

KuCoin did not mention its XMRUSDT perpetual contract in the notice. The contract had $33 million in 24-hour volume on Thursday, according to CoinMarketCap. Binance had the largest XMR perpetual market with $89.3 million.

PerpetualCow, who promotes the Wagyu trading platform on X, also responded to the delisting. "Over 50% of users sourced their XMR indirectly from KuCoin; it fuelled ALL instant swap exchanges," he wrote on Thursday. According to PerpetualCow, instant swap services "don't have their own liquidity" and "simply wrapped around KuCoin and sold/bought into their order books."

In the same post, he wrote that Wagyu had done more than $1.5 billion in volume in less than a year. He also shared a screenshot of Wagyu's XMR-USDC market together with the post, and it showed $63.5 million in 24-hour volume.

Earlier in November, the MEXC exchange also delisted XMR. The exchange removed XMR spot and perpetual markets on Nov. 13.

OKX delisted XMR in January 2024, and Binance removed the coin on Feb. 20, 2024. Binance said at the time that it would conduct a deeper review "when a coin or token no longer meets this standard, or the industry changes." XMR fell more than 15% after the Binance announcement.

Kraken stopped XMR trading for clients in the European Economic Area at the end of October 2024. In August 2025, Kraken announced an XMR delisting for Canadian clients "due to recent compliance requirements in Canada" and disabled trading for them on Sept. 2, 2025.

Solana is four days away from matching a record last seen in 2022. SOL has lost 25.7% in November so far (as of Nov. 26). That's likely to become the cryptocurrency's ninth losing month this year. If December also ends in the red, that would bring the total to 10, the highest number of losing months in a single year in SOL's history.

In terms of percentage losses, 2022 was overwhelmingly the worst year for Solana. SOL lost 94.15% in 2022. So far in 2026, it's down 43.09%.

SOL declined every month between January and July. August brought a 41.5% surge, followed by another 14.56% gain in September. Then, October and November erased all those gains.

As of Nov. 26, Bitcoin had fallen roughly 21% in November. That provides some context. In October, BTC dropped 7.32%, while SOL lost 19%. Solana was already underperforming Bitcoin before November's losses accelerated.

Meanwhile, another source of demand is faltering. U.S. spot Solana ETFs have recorded $164 million in net outflows over the 30 trading days leading up to Nov. 25.

On Nov. 6, investors withdrew about $24 million from these funds. By Nov. 25, when SOL was trading around $70, the funds recorded zero net inflows. Lower prices had not yet brought ETF investors back in significant numbers.

Solana's network activity actually grew during the summer rally. Quarterly trading volume on decentralized exchanges (DEXs) increased 23% from the previous quarter to $197 billion in Q3.

Of that, a record $7.1 billion came from tokenized equities. That's roughly 3.6% of the quarter's total volume.

Much of the third-quarter growth came from memecoins, according to Bitwise. On Nov. 26, the memecoin platform Pump accounted for $1.29 million of the $2.69 million in daily protocol revenue on Solana tracked by DefiLlama.

For SOL to recover and break even in November, it would need to rise about 34.6% by Nov. 30.

If November ends in the red, even a small decline in December would give Solana a record 10th losing month of the year.

December ended lower in five of the last six years shown on the chart. However, six data points aren't much to base a forecast on.

#5189. Enjin Matrixchain Votes on OpenGov Today: What Changes for ENJ Holders on November 16

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Enjin holders vote through November 13 on moving Matrixchain to OpenGov on November 16. Here is how the nine tracks, the 1,000 ENJ deposit and conviction voting work, and what the Relaychain vote shows.

Enjin's new proposal deposit sounds steep at 1,000 ENJ. It's actually the cheap part.

Enjin holders have until today, November 13, to vote on moving the Matrixchain to the Fort Canning release. The referendum opened November 10. If it passes, the upgrade is targeted for November 16 at block #12,319,600, with the network moving from runtime 1.3.1 to 1.4.3. Enjin's Fort Canning announcement lays out the plan, and the official changelog carries the technical detail.

The Relaychain has already made the jump. Referendum #16 approved its upgrade on October 28, and it went live on November 9. The Matrixchain vote is the second half of one upgrade, and it is the half that changes how Matrixchain makes decisions from then on.

Early coverage reported the schedule and the headline numbers: nine tracks, 1,000 ENJ. The changelog and the governance portal show the mechanics behind them, and those mechanics change more than the headlines suggest.

Today, the Matrixchain runs its governance through the older Democracy, Council and Technical Committee pallets, the modules that handle proposals and votes. Fort Canning replaces all three with a new set: Referenda, Conviction Voting, Origins, Whitelist and the Enjin Fellowship. Under OpenGov, any account can submit a referendum on one of nine tracks, and from the moment the upgrade lands, Matrixchain's own upgrades go through that process.

A track is a lane for a particular kind of decision. Enjin's changelog describes the families: Root and the admin tracks for the highest-stakes changes, Whitelisted Caller for proposals the Fellowship fast-tracks, and two special tracks, Referendum Killer and Referendum Canceller, for stopping a proposal that shouldn't proceed. Matrixchain gets no treasury tracks: those, sized by how much a proposal would spend, stay on the Relaychain, where treasury requests now go. Each track has its own deposit, approval curve and enactment period, and the Enjin Fellowship can fast-track time-sensitive proposals.

Splitting decisions this way means a small treasury request doesn't face the same bar as a change to the chain's core. Riskier tracks demand larger deposits and more support, while smaller ones move faster and cost less.

The submission deposit rises from 0.025 ENJ to 1,000 ENJ on every track, a 40,000-fold increase. The deposit is refunded when a referendum passes or is canceled, and it exists to deter spam. As an illustration, using the roughly $66 million market cap reported in early October, ENJ traded near three cents, which would put 1,000 ENJ around $33.

That is only the entry ticket. The cost that matters comes next. A referendum also needs a decision deposit before it moves into voting, and the changelog lists steep figures: 2,500,000 ENJ on Root and Fellowship Admin, 1,000,000 ENJ on the other admin tracks, and 2,500 to 250,000 ENJ on the Relaychain's treasury tracks. At the same illustrative price, the 2.5 million ENJ Root deposit comes to roughly $80,000, about 0.12% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance.

So proposing is cheap, and pushing a proposal through is not. Anyone can raise an idea, but anyone who wants the network to vote on something big needs real stake in the outcome. The changelog says the same values apply on both chains, and Matrixchain adopts them for its new tracks.

The best evidence of how these votes work comes from the Relaychain referendum that has already finished. Enjin's governance portal shows referendum #16 as finalised, approved on October 28 and enacted on November 9.

The final tally on the page is small. Eleven voters cast 381,303.02 ENJ of conviction-weighted voting power, and all of it went to Aye: 100% in favor, 0 ENJ against. The page also shows raw, unweighted support of 271,303.2 ENJ, which it describes as the total balance backing the proposal and the figure the support curve uses. The conviction multiplier on the page runs from under 1x up to 6x.

Two numbers stand out. First, an entire chain upgrade passed with 271,303 ENJ of raw support, about 0.013% of the 2.02 billion ENJ total issuance, a figure worked out from the portal's number. Second, conviction added about 110,000 ENJ of weight on top of the raw balance, an average multiplier of roughly 1.4x. Voters picked up some extra weight, but most didn't lock their tokens for the long periods that earn the top multipliers.

A 100% Aye result says little by itself. A scheduled upgrade with no organized opposition passes easily, and the tally shows how thin engagement was.

Fort Canning adds the safeguard that thin turnout calls for. A referendum now needs a minimum share of total ENJ voting in support. The changelog sets 0.5% on Root and the admin tracks, 0.005% to 0.125% on the Relaychain's treasury tracks, 0.1% for Referendum Killer and 0.05% for Referendum Canceller. Measured against 2.02 billion ENJ, that means about 10.1 million ENJ on Root, roughly 101,000 to 2.5 million on the treasury tracks, about 2.02 million to kill a referendum and about 1.01 million to cancel one.

Referendum #16's 271,303 ENJ of raw support would clear the lowest treasury floor of about 101,000 ENJ, but it would miss the Root floor by a factor of about 37. The page doesn't show which track the referendum used, and a runtime upgrade typically sits on a high-stakes track, so the Root comparison works as an illustration and not as a finding. The floors also didn't exist when #16 passed, since Fort Canning introduced them.

That is the real change. Under the new rules, 11 wallets can't carry a chain-level decision on their own. Low turnout means failure, and proposals that matter will need far more ENJ behind them. Enjin's changelog says Matrixchain upgrades go through OpenGov starting with this one, which suggests today's vote still runs on the current system, so the floors will first bite on the first OpenGov referendum.

Holders who haven't voted can still do so through Enjin's governance portal before the window closes. Voting locks tokens, so the lock length is worth checking first. Enjin's support article on voting explains the trade-off: the longer the lock, the more a vote counts, and tokens stay locked until the period ends.

Node operators on the Matrixchain can wait for the result before upgrading, as Enjin has indicated, and then follow the changelog for the version to install. Relaychain operators already needed client version 1.8.1.

This vote is more about control than speed. OpenGov spreads decisions across tracks with deposits and support floors built for the weight of each choice, and it moves ENJ holders from voting on a handful of items to a standing governance system. The Relaychain's first vote showed how little participation it took under the old rules, and the first referenda after November 16 will show whether holders turn out for the new ones. If most proposals stall at the decision deposit, the system costs too much. If they clear with a handful of voters, the floors aren't doing their job. Either result will tell holders what their ENJ can do.

The crypto markets have shown early signs of stabilization today, even as sentiment sits in extreme fear territory. Bitcoin has climbed back above $61,500 after a 1.9% gain over the past 24 hours, while the total market capitalization has reached $2.11 trillion with a 1.31% advance. The recovery has tracked gains in tech futures and commodities following the Thanksgiving holiday, with 24-hour crypto liquidations totaling $228.95 million (mostly in short positions) and open interest at $272.6 billion.

Spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded their largest monthly outflow on record, but BTC’s price bounce alongside broader risk assets points to resilience after recent volatility. The underlying strength in Bitcoin has also arrived as developers push forward with Layer 2 networks aimed at improving BTC’s transaction speed and expanding its practical uses.

This week’s most prominent BTC Layer 2 project, Bitcoin Hyper (HYPER), has finished its public presale campaign after raising $33.3 million. Buyers are now able to claim the HYPER tokens they purchased, and the token has been listed on Uniswap and Raydium. This project’s completed raise and progress toward a functional Layer 2 network position it to play a major role in Bitcoin’s evolution as the mainnet approaches.

Bitcoin Hyper (HYPER) is building a completely new Layer 2 network that processes transactions off Bitcoin’s main chain while anchoring final settlement back to the Layer 1. The L2 runs high-throughput operations through the SVM (Solana Virtual Machine), allowing near-instant finality for payments, DeFi activity, and decentralized applications.

Users will need to deposit native BTC to a monitored address; a smart contract then verifies the deposit against Bitcoin headers and proofs before minting an equivalent amount on the Layer 2. Batches of activity are compressed, protected by zero-knowledge proofs, and periodically committed to Bitcoin for security.

HYPER is the native token of the new L2, has a fixed supply of 21 billion, and functions as the gas token for fees on the network. Holders can also stake it to earn high-APY rewards. On the tokenomics side, allocations are 30% for development, 15% for rewards, 25% for the project’s treasury, 20% for marketing, and 10% for listings.

Hyper Mainnet is now secured by @hackenclub 🔓 ⚡ Read details 👇Hacken Portal: https://t.co/ruEFoCWHaTFinal Report: https://t.co/nSJy3Ys8mY pic.twitter.com/zY1ahvp7dQ

The public HYPER sale closed after collecting $33.3 million, supporting testnet components that are already operating, including the bridge, explorer, wallet, and staking portal. These elements form the base for full network operations, where the Layer 2 will handle faster transfers and smart-contract activity while relying on Bitcoin’s proof-of-work chain for final settlement. Audits by Coinsult and Spywolf (covering the HYPER token contract) and Hacken (covering L2 components) have also been completed.

Presale participants can now claim their HYPER tokens by first hard-refreshing the official Bitcoin Hyper site to clear the cache, then connecting the same wallet used for the original purchase. From there, they can choose either to claim the tokens directly or to claim and stake them at the same time.

Purchases made with Solana will be claimed on the Solana blockchain, while those completed with Ethereum, BNB, or a credit card can be claimed on Ethereum (contract addresses are specified on the official Bitcoin Hyper website). Once received, the tokens can be exchanged on Uniswap and Raydium.

Tokens that were staked during the presale become claimable starting December 3, and that date also marks the scheduled activation of the Layer 2 mainnet, which will include a dedicated wallet, transaction explorer, and bridge.

A complete list of HYPER claim instructions has been made available through an official Bitcoin Hyper X post:

Claiming is almost here! ⚡️🔥Full claim instructions on the official Hyper TG 👇https://t.co/iukXzZWfcX pic.twitter.com/6SneDFHPBO

This project’s now-completed capital raise and imminent network launch place Bitcoin Hyper in a strong position to deliver higher throughput and broader functionality for Bitcoin holders. With claims underway and mainnet activation days away, the project is advancing its plan to expand practical uses for the leading cryptocurrency.

Monero took a sharp hit on November 26, with the KuCoin Monero delisting announcement landing as XMR suffered its biggest single-day decline since June 4.

The timing is hard to ignore. But one exchange announcement doesn’t explain every sell order.

KuCoin confirmed it will close four XMR spot markets “XMR/USDT, XMR/USDC, XMR/ETH and XMR/BTC” at 08:00 UTC on November 30.

Other services face separate cutoffs. XMR Flexible Savings ends November 27 at 12:00 UTC, while Convert closes November 30 at 03:00 UTC. Trading bots stop at 06:00 UTC, followed by spot trading at 08:00 UTC.

Withdrawals are scheduled to remain available until December 31 at 08:00 UTC. Deposits are already closed. KuCoin says open orders will be cancelled when trading ends, while Flexible Savings balances and accrued earnings will move to Funding Accounts.

The exchange also warns withdrawals could be suspended earlier under certain project-related circumstances. It hasn’t provided a detailed reason for the removal.

KuCoin isn’t the only venue cutting Monero access. MEXC previously announced the removal of XMR spot pairs and later issued a separate notice covering XMR and DASH perpetual futures.

Those are different products. Spot markets provide access to the underlying asset, while perpetual contracts offer derivatives exposure.

Earlier Monero research from TRM Labs described liquidity becoming concentrated across fewer venues following exchange restrictions. That context matters, but it doesn’t establish how much of Thursday’s sell-off came from KuCoin.

Monero’s official account also announced an Eigenwallet release supporting Bitcoin and Monero, including native atomic swaps. These swaps allow users to exchange the assets without depositing both with a conventional exchange.

Still, a new trading route doesn’t automatically replace the depth of removed order books. The KuCoin Monero delisting leaves XMR facing a practical liquidity question as the deadlines approach.

#5184. NEAR’s Inflation Cut: The Math Behind a 5.27% to 3.37% Staking Yield

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

HSP-029 lowers NEAR’s issuance cap from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. The cap formula, the epoch step and the yield math show what that does to stakers.

Most headlines on NEAR’s new inflation schedule stop at “2.5% to 1.6%.” Stakers feel a different number. They earn about 5.27% today and will earn roughly 3.37% once the cut finishes, and a single line of arithmetic accounts for the gap.

House of Stake ratified HSP-029 on November 16, after the Security Council’s 14-day veto window passed without a veto. The proposal touches one parameter, the maximum annual issuance rate, which drops from 2.5% to 1.6% over 24 months. It is the second cut in just over a year, coming after the October 2025 halving from 5%.

Everything else stays put. Issuance still splits 90% to staking participants and 10% to the protocol treasury. There is no new spending program, no validator subsidy and no automatic trigger that could push issuance back up. The full proposal models 11.8 million NEAR of issuance avoided over two years and 66.1 million over six, measured against leaving the cap at 2.5%.

The schedule is a straight line with no stair steps:

Here t is the number of months since the reduction begins. The 0.9% is the total drop (2.5 minus 1.6), and dividing it by 24 gives a monthly step of 0.0375 percentage points, or 3.75 basis points. The min(t, 24) term caps the ramp at month 24, and the cap sits at 1.6% from there on.

NEAR applies the step every epoch rather than once a month. An epoch lasts about 12 hours, so the cap slips by roughly 0.0006 percentage points each time, far too little to notice on any given day. There are no step dates to mark on a calendar. Sampled every six months, the line looks like this:

The yield column uses the math in the next section. It drops about 0.08 percentage points a month, evenly, with no cliff.

New tokens go mostly to stakers, so the staked pool splits the reward, and a smaller pool earns more per token. That gives a working formula:

gross yield ≈ 0.9 × issuance cap ÷ staking ratio

The 0.9 is the staker share of issuance. Using the proposal’s figures, 0.9 × 2.5% ÷ 0.4271 comes to 5.27%, where 42.71% is the staking ratio reported when the proposal went to vote. Put in the 1.6% cap and 0.9 × 1.6% ÷ 0.4271 gives 3.37%, the same number the proposal publishes. Anyone can check the headline yields on a calculator.

The formula has two limits. It uses the cap, but realized issuance runs a little lower because transaction fees are burned. HSP-029 measured 2.45% in September, which puts today’s yield near 5.16%. The staking ratio also moves. When more people stake, the same rewards spread over more tokens and yield falls further, and when people unstake it climbs. The 3.37% figure assumes today’s ratio holds.

Stakers feel it first. By the proposal’s own math, someone staking 1,000 NEAR ends up with about 20 fewer tokens after two years than if the cap had stayed at 2.5%. The numbers back that up: yield averages about 4.32% across the ramp, roughly 0.95 points under today’s rate for two years.

Holders who don’t stake come out ahead. More than half of NEAR’s supply sits unstaked, and every new token dilutes those holdings. Trimming the cap by 0.9 percentage points trims that dilution by the same amount each year. Stakers give up some reward so that everyone else gives up less value.

Validators get an easier path than in 2025, when the halving cut staking rewards from about 9% to 4.75% in a single upgrade. Operators now have 24 months to plan. NEAR’s analysis finds that most validator revenue comes from commission on delegated stake, so service quality and fee competition shape income more than the issuance rate does.

Recent history explains the setup. When the 2025 halving shipped, an earlier community poll had missed the two-thirds threshold, and critics said the core team pushed the change through anyway. HSP-029 sidesteps that argument by design.

Two separate approvals are required. Token holders voting through veNEAR set the direction, and that vote closed November 2 with 99.96% in favor and none against. Validators then decide on their own whether to adopt the protocol upgrade that makes the cap binding. The author, Sal Ternullo of SVRN, opened discussion on October 7, and the process ran through the Screening Committee and Security Council in public. Raising issuance again would take a new proposal and another round of validator adoption, so nothing can be added quietly later.

Ratification does not change issuance yet. A one-quarter grace period comes first, giving wallets, exchanges, custodians and staking providers time to update their disclosures. NEAR One then releases the upgrade and validators choose whether to adopt it, with the reduction starting about a quarter after ratification. On schedule, that means a start in early 2027 and a 1.6% cap around early 2029.

Three things are worth tracking. Validator adoption of the upgrade comes first, because the cap stays at 2.5% until enough validators run it. The staking ratio comes next, since it moves yield regardless of the formula. Last are the quarterly transparency reports NEAR has promised, which compare realized issuance with the schedule.

Price is a separate question. Lower issuance eases supply pressure, but nothing in it creates demand. The cap will follow its published line down, and yield will follow the cap.

#5182. XRP Bulls and Bears to Get 3x ETFs Soon

Two proposed U.S. exchange-traded funds would give investors a way to bet on XRP in either direction, with one targeting three times XRP's daily return and the other targeting three times its inverse.

If XRP gains 5% in a single day, the bullish ETF would target a 15% gain, excluding fees and expenses.

If XRP loses 5% in a single day, the bearish ETF would target a 15% gain.

However, investors betting on the wrong direction could lose approximately 15% of their investment in a single day.

The next update is scheduled for Nov. 30. Following a recent amendment submitted to the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the registration statements for these ETFs are now scheduled to become effective on Monday.

The issuer has repeatedly delayed the effective date. It remains to be seen whether the funds will start trading anytime soon.

The filing covers a total of eight ETFs, including bullish and bearish funds for Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum (ETH), Solana (SOL) and XRP.

Even if XRP's price remains unchanged over multiple trading days, both ETFs could record negative returns.

Since the ETFs rebalance daily, it's important to remember that when the price changes direction, the next day's percentage return is calculated based on the investment's value after the previous trading session.

Let's say XRP rises from $2 to $2.20 on Monday and then drops back to $2 on Tuesday. If you hold XRP over these two days, you'll break even.

However, if you invest $100 in the bullish ETF, your position would close Tuesday at approximately $94.55, assuming the fund achieves its daily target and excluding fees and expenses.

If XRP increases by 10% from $2 to $2.20 on Monday, the bullish ETF would target a 30% gain. Your initial $100 investment would now be worth $130.

For XRP to return to $2 on Tuesday, it would need to fall by approximately 9.09%.

The bullish ETF would therefore target a loss of roughly 27.27% on Tuesday. But that loss would be calculated against your $130 position, leaving you with approximately $94.55.

Of course, the bearish ETF wouldn't fare any better.

#5181. Why Does AI Get Simple Questions Wrong? What Google's Humanity's First Exam Shows

You ask an AI model to name the color of the third letter in each word on a neon sign. It gets it right. You ask again, and it slips by one letter. Nothing broke.

The model could do the task. It just did not do it every time. Google DeepMind built a test for exactly that gap, and the results show how far "usually right" can sit from "reliably right."

Most AI benchmarks ask a model to solve a hard problem once. If it passes, it scores. Google DeepMind's Humanity's First Exam (HFE), released on November 24, 2026, asks something different. Can a model solve an easy task, and slight rewrites of it, every single time?

The prompts are elementary on purpose. They cover counting objects, naming colors, tracking where something moved, basic arithmetic, strict formatting rules and spotting false premises. Humans solve them in about a minute.

One public example: "List the color of the third letter of each word in the neon sign in order, separated by a semicolon." The answer is green; yellow; white; blue; blue.

The paper calls the difference the Family Reliability Gap. One slip anywhere in the 16 answers fails the whole family.

The top five models score 96% to 98% on a single try and 100% on family pass@4. Their family pass⁴ averages only 85.8%. Across all 18 models, the gap runs from 7.6 to 80.1 percentage points.

The bottom row is the sharpest case. That model gets 68.7% of single tries right, yet clears only 18.6% of question families every time. Its family pass@4 is 98.8%, so it could solve nearly every family at least once.

The math is simple. Say a model is right 90% of the time on each answer, and the answers are independent. Getting 16 in a row right happens about 18.5% of the time (0.9 to the 16th power). That is a rough illustration, not the paper's calculation, but it shows how small error rates compound.

The paper's own example makes the same point. One model trails the leader by 6.6 points on single tries and by 29.4 points on family pass⁴. On average, about half the shortfall comes from prompts a model always fails. The other half comes from flakiness: right on some runs, wrong on others.

Humans and models also struggle in opposite places. People were least accurate on math and logic seeds. Models were strongest there and weakest on counting and reading text inside images.

Traders now hand AI tools real jobs: reading a contract, summarizing a token page, checking a wallet address in a screenshot, or running a bot. In those jobs, one wrong character or one miscounted number is the whole failure. A model that is right 19 times out of 20 will still be wrong on the 20th, and a signed transaction cannot be undone.

1. Ask twice. Run the same question more than once. If the answers differ, treat both as unconfirmed.

2. Check the visual parts yourself. Counts, colors, positions and text read from an image are where models slip most. Compare addresses and numbers character by character against the original.

3. Match the effort to the task. More reasoning helps with text and math. It helps little with images, so do not assume a longer "thinking" mode makes a screenshot read safe.

4. Keep a human on irreversible steps. Sending funds, signing transactions and changing settings should not rest on a single AI answer.

#5180. Bitcoin Miners Go 98 Minutes Without Finding a Single Block

Bitcoin miners experienced their longest dry spell since July on Nov. 26. According to Galaxy's Alex Thorn, it took Bitcoin miners 98 minutes and 19 seconds to find the next block.

That's the third time in 2026 that miners have gone this long without finding a block. The wait ended at 18:28 UTC on Thursday.

For anyone trying to get Bitcoin transactions confirmed shortly after the previous block, the gap meant waiting more than an hour and a half.

Even if you paid a very high transaction fee, you would still have to wait until a miner found the next block before your transaction could receive its first confirmation.

Thursday's gap was the 69th longest since 2011, according to Galaxy Research. It was just three minutes shy of the threshold for the top 50.

And this year's other long gap lasted nearly two hours. On July 6, miners took 112 minutes and 26 seconds to find the next block (number 956,953). That was the 19th longest gap on record, according to Galaxy.

Bitcoin automatically adjusts mining difficulty every 2,016 blocks to keep the average block interval at around 10 minutes.

However,  blocks sometimes are found seconds apart. Other times, it takes well over an hour for the next block to be found.

At any given mining difficulty, the chance that a single attempt to find a block will succeed is incredibly small.

If miners have spent 90 minutes trying to find the next block, the chance of succeeding on the next attempt is the same as it was on the first attempt.

So the expected time until the next block is found is still 10 minutes, even if it's already been 90 minutes since the last block was found. That's assuming the network's total computing power and mining difficulty remain unchanged.

Assuming an average block interval of 10 minutes, Thorn said you could expect a gap of at least 98 minutes and 19 seconds about once every 18,600 block intervals.

That means such a gap should occur roughly once every four months, based on an average of about 144 blocks per day.

Galaxy examined 877,290 block intervals going back to Jan. 1, 2011.

Researchers identified 1,948 intervals where at least an hour had passed between the timestamps of successive blocks.

However, Galaxy flagged 97 of those intervals because an adjacent block had a timestamp that was off by at least 10 minutes. This raised questions about the actual length of those gaps.

The longest recorded interval is particularly interesting.

On Nov. 30, 2011, block 155,290 seemingly marked the end of a 144-minute-and-50-second gap.

However, the miner who found the next block had set its timestamp back by 65 minutes.

After excluding apparent timestamp errors, the longest gap was 141 minutes and one second, recorded on Oct. 13, 2011.

SingleAssetVault activation is projected for December 9, subject to continued validator support.

XRPL stablecoin supply reached $836.90 million, with RLUSD representing 89.35%.

The proposed lending system supports uncollateralised loans, while borrower underwriting remains offchain.

The XRP Ledger lending system is getting closer to deployment, but don’t confuse a countdown with a working loan market. The SingleAssetVault amendment is projected to activate on December 9, provided validator support holds. The separate LendingProtocol amendment still needs approval.

Meanwhile, XRPL stablecoin supply has reached $836.90 million. RLUSD accounts for 89.35% of that total, according to November 27 figures. That’s a sizeable balance, but it isn’t money already committed to lending.

The SingleAssetVault amendment would establish infrastructure for pooling a single asset and issuing depositors shares representing their interest. The LendingProtocol amendment performs a different job: it enables brokers to arrange fixed-term loans and record repayments on the ledger.

XRPL amendments need more than 80% support from trusted validators for two consecutive weeks. If support falls short, the waiting period can restart. So December 9 remains a projection, not a guaranteed launch date.

The proposed system supports uncollateralised loans, making borrower assessment a serious issue for depositors. Underwriting and risk management happen offchain, according to the lending specification.

Brokers may also contribute optional first-loss capital in the same asset as the loan pool. That can absorb some missed-payment losses, but it isn’t a blanket guarantee.

The XRP Ledger Foundation has published an open-source reference application demonstrating the system on Devnet. It combines vaults and lending with credentials, permissioned domains and batch transactions.

Still, a working demonstration isn’t commercial adoption. XRPL DeFi total value locked stands at about $30.65 million, a separate measure from the $836.94 million stablecoin balance.

The XRP Ledger lending system now needs amendment activation, production markets and funded loans before stablecoin supply can translate into actual lending activity.

#5170. Bitcoin News Today: BTC Rebounds 8% – Is The Worst Over for Bitcoin Holders?

Bitcoin news today: BTC bounces 8% with gold and silver after Thanksgiving. Since 2013, only New Year shows a reliable gain.

In Bitcoin news today, November 27, BTC USD price climbed back to $61,780 after Thanksgiving, up 8% from Wednesday’s low of $57,300. Gold and silver bounced even harder, as the dollar weakened in thin holiday trading.

BREAKING: Bitcoin reclaims $62,000 after jumping +8.5% in just 2 days.

$150 BILLION added to crypto market over the same period. pic.twitter.com/aMW3gcwKJW

— Bull Theory (@BullTheoryio) November 27, 2026

The rebound barely dents a brutal month. Bitcoin is still down 20% in November, from $77,580 on November 1. So is this a Thanksgiving pump, and does Bitcoin have a holiday-season pattern? We checked every Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year since 2013.

The answer is mostly no. Bitcoin rose over Thanksgiving weekend in only 6 of 13 years, and over Christmas in 5 of 13.

Is there no correlation at all? New Year is the exception: Bitcoin gained between December 30 and January 2 in 12 of the last 13 years.

All three assets rebounded after a rough Wednesday, when hot inflation data sealed a December Fed rate hike. Bitcoin rose 8% from its $57,300 low to $61,780, its highest level since Monday.

The metals moved faster. US gold futures climbed 4.6% from Wednesday’s close to $3,699 an ounce. Silver did even better, jumping 11.4% to $44.60. Analysts tied the rebound to a weaker US dollar.

The timing matters. US markets were closed on Thursday and trade only half a day on Friday, so thin volume made every move look bigger.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Best Low-Cap Crypto

To put Bitcoin news today in context, we measured bitcoin’s price change in three holiday windows every year from 2013 to 2025, using Bitstamp’s daily closing prices.

Thanksgiving weekend, from Wednesday’s close to Sunday’s, has been a coin flip. Bitcoin rose in 6 of 13 years, and the median move was -0.1%. The swings were large in both directions, from a 13.2% drop in 2018 to 12.9% gains in 2015 and 2017.

Christmas was no better. Between December 23 and 26, bitcoin rose in only 5 of 13 years, again with a median move of -0.1%.

New Year stands out. From December 30 to January 2, bitcoin gained in 12 of the last 13 years, with a median rise of 1.8%. The only drop came in 2019. The gain is small, but it keeps repeating, perhaps because some funds and traders put fresh cash to work at the start of the year.

EXPLORE: BTC News Today: US Bitcoin Strategic Reserve Bill Moves Closer as BTC Reclaims $60K

From the day before Thanksgiving to January 2, Bitcoin rose in 7 of 13 years, and the size of the move tracked its four-year cycle. In bull years the season was spectacular: bitcoin gained 79% in 2017 and 72% in 2020. In the years after a cycle top, it disappointed, with 14% drops in both 2014 and 2018 and a flat season in 2022.

The gains also tended to fade once the holidays ended. Bitcoin fell in January in 8 of 13 years, with a median drop of 5.4%.

This year looks more like the post-top years. Bitcoin peaked in October 2025 and is down more than half since. So for Bitcoin news today, the lesson is that a holiday bounce has not yet changed the trend.

BTC trades at $61,780, below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $71,180, and its 200-day EMA at $74,450.

The takeaway from Bitcoin news today: history says the Thanksgiving bounce is a coin flip, and the season as a whole follows the cycle. If the pattern holds, the one date worth watching is the turn of the year.

#5169. Binance Announces Dividends for Nvidia and Other Stocks

Binance will pay dividends to holders of stock tokens representing five companies: Nvidia, PayPal, Qualcomm, Western Digital, and Wendy’s.

The exchange will use the dividends paid by these companies to buy more stock tokens, allowing users to increase their holdings of the same stocks through the bStocks program.

The most important date for Nvidia token holders is Dec. 2. That's when Binance will take a snapshot of NVDAB balances at 01:00 UTC.

The snapshot for Wendy’s is scheduled for Dec. 1, followed by Nvidia on Dec. 2 and Qualcomm on Dec. 3.

Snapshots for PayPal and Western Digital are both scheduled for Dec. 4.

All snapshots will take place at 01:00 UTC.

In its Nov. 27 announcement, Binance provided the dates that will determine eligibility for dividends.

Binance plans to use Nvidia's cash dividends to purchase additional Nvidia shares, including fractional shares, after deducting applicable withholding taxes, fees, and other charges.

The proceeds will then be distributed among users who hold NVDAB on Binance and qualify for the dividend payment.

The same process will apply to the other four stocks.

If you hold eligible tokens in other products on the platform, such as savings or margin accounts, Binance will still credit the dividends to your spot account.

If you hold bStocks on-chain, the dividend payments will be made by adjusting the token's multiplier.

The tokens themselves are issued by Binance affiliate BTECH Holdings Limited, which owns the underlying securities.

So, if you hold NVDAB, you have an interest in the Nvidia shares held by BTECH.

If you need to transfer tokens to Binance before the snapshot, you must do so at least two hours in advance.

Deposits and withdrawals of Nvidia tokens will be suspended at 23:00 UTC on Dec. 1.

Binance will also suspend one-to-one conversions between Nvidia shares and NVDAB tokens during this period.

The same two-hour suspension rule will apply to the other four stock tokens.

However, spot trading against USDT will continue, including trading in the NVDAB/USDT pair.

Binance said it would resume deposits, withdrawals, and stock-to-token conversions after the dividend allocations are completed.

The exchange will not issue a separate announcement when these services resume.

#5166. SWIFT Weighs XRP & ALGO Benefits vs. Quantum Threats

Home » Ripple (XRP) » SWIFT Weighs XRP & ALGO Benefits vs. Quantum Threats

PQC algorithms deliver the same core functions like regular cryptography, but absorb the quantum-computing hazards.

SWIFT, the largest European financial conglomerate, has just released their latest perspective on quantum computing threats, a topic the crypto community, including the XRP Army, has eagerly debated over the past few months.

The financial community is uniting towards building the post-quantum cryptography (PQC) service, which would replace the algorithms prone to breaking by quantum computing. This aligns with the roadmap of several DLT-based altcoins, including Ripple (XRP) & Algorand (ALGO).

Both of these Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) based chains are preparing for signatures that erases those threats, potentially fully implementing it by 2028. “Today’s cryptography is deeply embedded across systems, applications & processes”, – the paper states, carving out a transitional path.

Transitioning to new standards requires SWIFT compliant organisations to understand where they are exposed and manage change in a controlled, resilient way. Blockchain adoption comes as a no-brainer: SWIFT’s new ledger acts as a plug between multiple popular chains, including Ripple’s XRP.

Q-Day is coming. Are we ready?Quantum computing could reshape the foundations of financial security as we know them.Preparing for that future starts now, and it will take the financial community working together.In the latest article in our Perspectives series, Michael… pic.twitter.com/kjLteDKFeM

SWIFT’s statement urges companies not to wait for complete inventory of cryptographic assets, but rather prioritise their most critical and exposed systems, beginning the PQC transition. That’s where Algorand (ALGO) & Ripple’s XRP Ledger stands out from the regular crypto crowd. Algorand’s is leading the pack.

The chain’s workable quantum-proof mechanics are being gradually implemented from 2022, targeting broad quantum resilience by the last quarter of 2027. This includes more account features, multisig & solid research into a post-quantum VRF and consensus messaging. First Falcon-protected transfers hit the mainnet in 2025.

It already protects historical state and offers native quantum-resistant accounts that people can use today. On XRP’s part, the Ledger sports a well-documented, institution-oriented plan with a practical migration path (keeping the same address, dropping the old key) with a mid 2028 goal. However, that’s still pre-development aspirations.

🚨 Many people may not truly grasp the full picture when it comes to SWIFT!Why do people keep linking various cryptocurrencies to SWIFT?Here’s the key: the logic centers on three distinct roles:🔥 XRP = LiquidityFacilitates the flow of funds, enabling the rapid transfer of… pic.twitter.com/hh4a1zhj0w

Algorand’s better matched with SWIFT POC aspirations for now. XRP currently uses classical elliptic-curve signatures, known as secp256k1 / Ed25519. No post-quantum signatures are live on the Ledger’s mainnet. The high-standard approach is going to be tested in 2027, while SWIFT is already piloting a roster of Ripple-linked banks.

Santander, Standard Chartered, HSBC & Deutsche Bank are the highlights of a double-digit list, but that doesn’t necessarily mean XRP coin is used as collateral or settlement. The chain’s On-Demand Liquidity (ODL) provides an additional liquidity layer via XRP, but it’s optional.

The bigger question is whether XRP can become a standard settlement layer on cross-border corridors.

#5165. Bank of Japan Warns Stablecoins and Tokenization Threaten Financial Stability

Japan's central bank has warned that automated trading in tokenized markets could exacerbate a sell-off.

It also raised concerns about whether stablecoin holders can always redeem their tokens at face value.

A Bank of Japan executive director outlined these risks during his keynote speech at an International Monetary Fund seminar in Tokyo.

In the event of a price drop, according to Kazushige Kamiyama, a smart contract could automatically increase the amount of collateral required. It could also trigger a sale of the collateral backing a position if the borrower doesn't have enough collateral.

These sales could drive prices even lower, potentially spreading financial stress across institutions and markets.

In the case of stablecoins, the question is whether a token with a face value of one dollar can always be redeemed for one dollar.

To ensure this, issuers' reserves need to be properly regulated, and the links to central bank money need to be reliable, Kamiyama said.

A bank might have enough cash to pay for a trade in tokenized assets but still be unable to complete the payment.

This could happen when a trade is settled overnight, and the payment system the bank uses to transfer cash is unavailable.

The bank might have to keep additional cash on a trading platform. Meanwhile, cash held on another network might not be accessible when the payment is due.

"Even with faster settlement, it does not necessarily lead to efficient liquidity management," Kamiyama said.

Cross-border securities trades, however, could benefit from tokenization.

A smart contract could link the payment and delivery of a security so that both transactions are executed simultaneously.

This could reduce the risk of a buyer paying for an asset without receiving it.

The Bank of Japan is setting up a testing environment with financial institutions that hold accounts at the central bank.

One scenario involves exploring how cash settlement could work for trades involving tokenized Japanese government bonds.

The central bank is considering two options for making the cash payment.

One would involve issuing tokenized central bank money. The other would link a token trading platform to Japan's existing payment infrastructure.

These tests will evaluate whether the proposed solutions can address the challenges financial institutions face when settling trades.

Monero (XMR) is not welcome on top exchanges as the series of delistings takes an uglier turn for holders following Kucoin's XMR removal. But Kucoin wasn't first and might not be the last: XMR was removed from MEXC, Kraken, Binance and others already.

The main issue for an asset that's being removed from exchanges will always be the liquidity. In the last 24 hours, Monero's spot flow lost $1.3 million. Despite the increasing volume, the asset is recording outflows and exchange withdrawals. The volume spike is most like being a reflection of a substantial selling activity.

In a single day, XMR was losing almost 20% of its value. If it wasn't for the delisting, price could've broken multiple technical resistances already and confirmed a recovery. As of November 27, the price is slowly recovering, following the general relief on the cryptocurrency market.

On November 26, Kucoin announced the removal of XMR/USDT, XMR/USDC, XMR/ETH and XMR/BTC trading pairs, effective November 30. The exchange has already limited any deposits, with withdrawals available for all users.

Monero is an inherently private cryptocurrency, that limits the ability of explorers to determine transaction destination and senders. That is the main reason centralized exchanges are removing XMR.

For holders, the problem is not that Monero stops working after a delisting. The network is still active, and XMR can be transferred between wallets or traded on exchanges that continue to support it. The problem is that there are fewer places to buy and sell it. If more large exchanges follow Kucoin, liquidity could become lower, making new selling activity more painful for the price.

XRP is approaching a price level it has repeatedly failed to reclaim. According to the latest Ripple news, the token climbed 3.6% to $0.978 on November 27, putting $1 back within reach for the sixth time in two weeks.

The token has a busy week of Ripple updates behind it. Ripple signed a Turkish bank as a custody client, and its RLUSD stablecoin reached a record supply. Spot XRP ETFs, which hold the token itself, drew fresh money. XRP Ledger validators also moved closer to switching on a lending feature.

XRP needs the help. It is down 56% from a year ago and has lost more than a fifth of its value since the start of November.

The question is whether this Ripple news is enough to push XRP back through $1. Our check of the daily chart shows why the level matters so much.

The largest piece of Ripple news came on Wednesday. Ripple announced that Yapı Kredi, one of Türkiye’s largest private banks, will use Ripple Custody to hold crypto for its trading arm. On the XRP Ledger, the network that XRP runs on, validators are close to approving a bank-style lending system. A vault feature could go live on December 9. The lending upgrade, which validators must vote on, is one vote short of the support it needs.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Predicts Next Crypto to Hit 1 Dollar

To see why $1 matters, we went through XRP’s daily candles on Binance since June.

The level held XRP up for most of the summer. XRP touched $1 in late June and again for two weeks in August, and buyers stepped in each time. After a brief dip in mid-August, it then closed above $1 for 89 days in a row, from August 17 to November 13.

That streak ended on November 14, when XRP fell 10% in a day. Since then the old floor has acted as a ceiling. XRP’s daily high reached or came within a cent of $1 on November 14, 17, 18, 19 and 23, and every time sellers pushed it back. The highest attempt, on Monday, briefly hit $1.026 before XRP closed at $0.94.

Binance’s order book shows the wall too. On Friday afternoon, sell orders worth about $700,000 sat at $1.00, more than double the orders at $0.99.

XRP trades at $0.978, below its 50-day exponential moving average (EMA), an average that gives recent prices more weight, at $1.13, and its 200-day EMA at $1.29.

Market Intelligence: Crypto Analyst Reveals Upcoming Coinbase Listings

This week’s Ripple news gives XRP more reasons to rally than it had a month ago. But the chart has the final say, and the first daily close above $1 since November 13 is the signal to wait for.

#5158. Ripple's David Schwartz Shuts Down XRP Escrow Burn Idea: Even 80% Can’t Force It

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

Ripple CTO Emeritus David Schwartz said on Friday that XRP Ledger validators cannot force the rest of the network to burn Ripple's escrowed XRP, even with more than 80% support. According to Schwartz, the XRP Ledger has "no coercive mechanism at all."

Schwartz, one of the creators of the XRP Ledger, made the comments in two replies on X on Thursday and Friday. The thread started on Wednesday with a post from an XRP community member. According to the post, "validators have no say over Ripple's escrow," and Ripple runs one validator on the default Unique Node List (dUNL), not three.

Another X user then asked: "Couldn't validators pass an amendment that would burn Ripple's escrow? Changes to the code of the XRPL could do anything..." Schwartz answered on Thursday that such validators would "just disagree with everyone else who didn't want that change and be counted as disagreeing validators, effectively isolating themselves from the network."

If the majority of nodes want something, nothing can stop them from having it. They just can't force those who don't agree to go along with them. But the same is true for a minority of nodes too. There's no coercive mechanism at all.

On Friday, the same user asked whether the answer would change if "the vast majority (80+%)" wanted the burn. "If the majority of nodes want something, nothing can stop them from having it. They just can't force those who don't agree to go along with them. But the same is true for a minority of nodes too. There's no coercive mechanism at all," Schwartz wrote.

On Nov. 16, a group of XRP holders called Make XRP Great Again demanded in an open letter to Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse that the company burn 31.1 billion escrowed XRP by March 31, 2027. XRP Insights recorded the same amount in 99 escrow objects that day. Ripple reported 31.7 billion XRP in escrow as of Sept. 30.

According to XRPScan, an amendment on the XRP Ledger needs 29 of 35 validator votes, or more than 80%, and has to keep that support for two weeks before it activates.

In late 2020, Schwartz wrote on X that "if the majority wants a rules change, there is nothing the minority can do to stop them." On Feb. 19, 2024, he wrote that Ripple "could unilaterally create the same effect as burning an escrow by provably blackholing the account the escrow completes into."

In February 2026, Schwartz argued with Cyber Capital founder Justin Bons on X. Bons called the XRP Ledger centralized and said that its Unique Node List gives Ripple control over consensus. Schwartz described the claims as "objectively nonsensical."

Ripple's next monthly escrow release of 1 billion XRP is scheduled for Dec. 1. In its Nov. 16 letter, Make XRP Great Again also asked Garlinghouse for a public response and a verifiable plan for the burn.

In a recent turn of events, Fidelity Investments filed a Form S-1 registration statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to launch a spot Chainlink [LINK] exchange-traded product (ETP).

According to the 25th November filing, the proposed fund is expected to trade on Nasdaq under the provisional ticker FLNK. That said, the fund would also hold LINK tokens directly. This allows investors to gain exposure to LINK through traditional stock market accounts without having to purchase or manage the tokens themselves.

At the same time, the fund aims to track the Fidelity Chainlink Reference Rate, which calculates LINK’s price using a volume-weighted median methodology based on data from eligible spot markets.

Notably, its holdings would be managed by three proposed custodians, including Anchorage Digital Bank, BitGo Bank & Trust, and Coinbase Custody Trust Company.

As expected, this news did have a positive impact on LINK’s price, which was trading at $9.16 at press time after a hike of 5.5% in the past 24 hours. With this, Fidelity becomes the third asset manager to launch a LINK ETF besides Grayscale’s GLNK and Bitwise’s CLNK.

In fact, according to SoSo Value data, GLNK and CLNK have already recorded cumulative net inflows of $128.12 million and $47.88 million, respectively. This in turn has brought their combined cumulative inflows to approximately $176 million. However, neither fund recorded any new flows on the 25th of November, with both showing $0 in daily net inflows.

This news comes as the broader cryptocurrency investment products recorded widespread outflows across major digital assets in the month of November. Starting with Bitcoin [BTC] ETFs, which witnessed the largest withdrawals, worth approximately $5.39 billion in net outflows, facing their worst month since launch.

Ethereum [ETH] ETFs too saw $1.30 billion worth of outflows. This was followed by XRP ETFs, which saw $29.18 million in outflows, while Solana [SOL] ETFs registered withdrawals of $57 million. Meanwhile, Dogecoin [DOGE] ETFs recorded relatively smaller outflows of $409,130.

Interestingly, not all products experienced negative flows, as HBAR ETFs attracted approximately $1.71 million in net inflows. This made it the only asset in the sea of ETFs to record positive flows on the day.

The European Commission’s 22nd sanctions package against Russia extends the European Union’s (EU) transaction ban to over 60 Russian banks and says all 60 of those will be removed from SWIFT, President Ursula von der Leyen said in Strasbourg on 23 November 2026.

While focusing on Russian SWIFT sanctions, the EU added 51 entities to the anti-circumvention list, while the majority of them, 27, were outside Russia: 14 came from China, including four in Hong Kong, four in Türkiye, three in Kyrgyzstan, two in India, two in Kazakhstan and two more in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

The European Union (EU) freshly assembled the Crypto Task Force to counter new crypto-related ways of evading the huge pile of sanctions, including limitations of Russian business abroad via ‘third-world’ parties. The Council will decide when the ban enters into force, after the necessary measures are activated.
